Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks

Vishesh Karwa*† vishesh.karwa@temple.edu Affiliation: Edoardo M. Airoldi*† edoardo.airoldi@temple.edu Affiliation: Donald B. Rubin*†‡ rubin@stat.harvard.edu Affiliation: *Department of Statistics, Operations, and Data Science, Temple University Affiliation: †Data Science Institute, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA 19122, USA Affiliation: ‡Department of Statistics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA
Abstract

Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment–spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment–exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz–Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.

1 Introduction

Under treatment interference, the potential outcome of one unit may depend on the treatment assignments of other units in the finite population. Consequently, the table of science is exponentially large. Moreover, unlike the classical case of no interference, there is no unique canonical causal estimand like the average treatment effect. Thus causal inference under interference requires assumptions on the structure of the table of science, together with a specification of a causal estimand and a design and estimator used to learn the estimand.

A large literature has emerged for causal inference under interference across settings such as peer effects (Manski, 1993; Bramoullé et al., 2009; Graham, 2008), vaccination studies (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008), spatial environments (Zigler et al., 2012; Giffin et al., 2023), and online and network experiments (Aral and Walker, 2011). These approaches use a variety of assumptions to reduce the number of potential outcomes per unit and define different causal estimands along with designs and estimators to estimate them. However, two layers of the causal inference problem are often specified jointly, sometimes even implicitly. The first concerns the modeling assumptions on potential outcomes. Assumptions under interference involve three distinct choices: which units’ treatment assignments in the finite population may affect a given unit’s potential outcome, how those assignments are summarized or aggregated, and what functional restrictions, if any, are imposed on the resulting potential outcomes. These choices correspond to interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models respectively. These three modeling assumptions are often conflated in the literature, but they play different mathematical roles.

The second layer concerns the definition of causal effects and its interaction with design and estimation. Some causal estimands under interference are fixed potential-outcome contrasts: they compare outcomes under two specified treatment allocations or treatment–exposure conditions. Other estimands are allocation-averaged contrasts: they average potential outcomes under a specified allocation distribution, often corresponding to a policy implementation. We treat the allocation distribution that is part of the definition of an estimand as distinct from the design used to estimate it.

Without separating these layers, it can be difficult to determine whether differences across methods arise from different assumptions on the potential-outcome table, different causal estimands, different allocation policies, different experimental designs, or different estimators. In this paper, we develop a unified framework for finite population causal inference under interference that makes these distinctions explicit. We consider the Table of Science as the primitive finite-population object. We develop a set of hierarchical modeling assumptions on the Table of Science in the form of interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. The first two are exclusion restrictions: they reduce the Table of Science by declaring which assignment coordinates can matter and which assignments are equivalent. On the other hand, an outcome model is a functional restriction on the potential outcomes. Once an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping are specified, the full-assignment potential outcome Yi​(𝐳)Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}) is represented by a lower-dimensional reduced potential outcome Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e), where 𝐳\mathbf{z} is the vector of treatment allocations, ziz_{i} is unit ii’s treatment, and eie_{i} is its exposure. A central consequence of this representation is a nonparametric linear decomposition of the reduced potential outcome Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e) given by

Yi​(z,e)=Ai​(z)+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e),Y_{i}(z,e)=A_{i}(z)+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e),

where AiA_{i} captures the direct treatment component, BiB_{i} the spillover component, and CiC_{i} the treatment–spillover interaction. This decomposition is a reparameterization of the potential outcomes. It gives a common language for specifying nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric finite population models of potential outcomes under interference. For example, a nonparametric model can leave the exposure as the full interference neighborhood and leave Ai,Bi,CiA_{i},B_{i},C_{i} unrestricted. Semiparametric and parametric outcome models impose additional restrictions such as additivity, homogeneity, linearity in exposure, or parametric forms for the spillover and interaction components. All potential-outcome models used in the interference literature, including arbitrary interference, linear-in-means models, stratified interference, binary exposure, spatial decay, and threshold or contagion models, can be represented within this hierarchy by appropriate choices of the interference neighborhood, exposure mapping, and outcome-model restrictions.

The framework also separates two natural classes of causal estimands under interference, assuming that the interference neighborhood and exposure mappings are correctly specified. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as the direct and total treatment effects, are contrasts of fixed potential outcomes under specific treatment allocations or treatment–exposure combinations. They are properties of the finite population and do not involve an allocation distribution. In contrast, expected causal effects (ECEs), such as the expected direct effect (EDE) and expected indirect effect (EIE), are contrasts of expectations of potential outcomes under allocation distributions–sometimes also referred to as policies. The distributions entering the two arms of the contrast may be the same, different, or induced by a common allocation rule; in all cases, the allocation distribution used to average potential outcomes is part of the causal question itself. The experimental design remains distinct from this allocation distribution, though it is usually informed by it.

We show that there is a fundamental separation between the two classes for nonparametric estimation. For ACEs, the design must reveal the particular treatment–exposure potential outcomes that define the target estimand. Potential outcomes revealed by the design but outside this set are nuisance for that estimand: without further outcome-model restrictions on the causal response surface, observing them gives no information about the fixed target potential outcomes. For ECEs, by contrast, the exposure states generated by the target allocation distribution enter the estimand. The design does not need to isolate a set of fixed treatment-exposure conditions; it must reproduce the allocation distribution’s averaging weights.

We illustrate this through design-based variance bounds for canonical weighted unbiased Horvitz–Thompson estimators. We show that, for both classes of estimands, the variance of the canonical estimator decomposes into a diagonal weight term, an interference-dependence term from overlapping neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term induced by the randomization design. The difference lies in the weight term. ACE weights involve design-induced inverse propensity scores for fixed relevant treatment–exposure conditions. Under classical graph-unaware designs, these propensity scores can be exponentially small in the degree of the interference graph, and matching lower bounds show that this obstruction applies to all unbiased estimators. By contrast, ECE weights are allocation policy-to-design importance weights; when the design is aligned with the allocation policy, the diagonal term is mild and the dominant cost is the dependence among observed weighted outcomes. Consequently we show that, under the same classical designs, fixed treatment-exposure ACE estimation can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the degree of the interference graph, whereas ECE estimation is limited by polynomial dependence on the degree of an appropriate dependence graph.

These results have direct practical implications for design and estimation. Designs for nonparametric ACE estimation must be aligned with the treatment–exposure combinations that define the target estimand. Potential outcomes that do not appear in the definition of the estimand are nuisance potential outcomes for nonparametric estimation. Thus, nonparametric estimation of ACEs requires specialized graph-aware designs that place sufficient probability on revealing the relevant potential outcomes. We construct such designs from independent sets of the interference graph: a distance-one independent-set design targets the direct treatment effect and a distance-two independent-set design targets the total treatment effect. We show that in each case, these graph aware designs replace the exponentially small propensity of the relevant potential outcome by a focal probability that is polynomial in the relevant local graph size. Sparse seeding of the distance-one independent set additionally estimates the influencer spillover effect—the average effect of treated influencers on untreated peers under the any-treated exposure map—at constant-order focal propensities on locally tree-like regular graphs (Section 5.3). The resulting estimators have mean squared error polynomial in the graph degree scale for broad graph classes. For the total effect, cluster randomized designs can be sharper than the independent-set construction when closed neighborhoods are contained in few clusters, though this requires the clustering to be aligned with the interference graph. Outcome-model restrictions provide another route for ACE estimation by relating nuisance potential outcomes to target potential outcomes, but this route is no longer fully nonparametric and is subject to misspecification of the outcome model. By contrast, for ECEs, the allocation policy is part of the estimand itself, and all potential outcomes with positive probability under the policy enter the estimand. Thus, ECEs can be estimated nonparametrically under classical Bernoulli designs when the target allocation policy is Bernoulli.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the Table of Science and the modeling hierarchy. Section 2.3 gives the non-parametric decomposition of Potential Outcomes and shows how common model classes arise as special cases. Section 3 defines ACEs and ECEs. Section 4 develops the generic estimation bounds and the ACE/ECE bottleneck comparison. Section 6 draws implications for classical estimators, specialized designs, and model-assisted estimation. Section 5 develops estimand-aligned independent-set designs that recover polynomial rates for average causal effects—including a sparse-seeding design that estimates the influencer spillover effect at constant-order propensities on bounded-degree graphs—together with a comparison against cluster randomized designs, and Section 8 concludes.

2 Hierarchical models of potential outcomes

Consider a finite population of nn units, indexed by i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, and a binary treatment assignment zi∈{0,1}z_{i}\in\{0,1\} for each unit ii. The vector of treatment assignments is denoted by 𝐳=(z1,…,zn)\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\dots,z_{n}), with 𝐳∈{0,1}n\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}. Under arbitrary treatment interference, the potential outcome of a unit ii depends on the entire assignment vector. We write

Yi​(𝐳),𝐳∈{0,1}n.Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}),\qquad\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

This denotes the full-assignment potential outcome of unit ii under treatment allocation 𝐳\mathbf{z}. The collection of all full-assignment potential outcomes

𝕋={Yi(𝐳):i=1,…,n,𝐳∈{0,1}n}\mathbb{T}=\{Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}):i=1,\dots,n,\ \mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\}

is the Table of Science for the study. Crucially, 𝕋\mathbb{T} is a fixed, full n×2nn\times 2^{n} table dictated by nature, existing prior to any modeling assumptions. Let 𝐙\mathbf{Z} denote the random treatment assignment generated by a design p⁡(𝐙)p(\mathbf{Z}). The observed outcome for unit ii is

Yiobs=Yi​(𝐙),Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),

and in any realized experiment, exactly one column of 𝕋\mathbb{T} is observed.

Since each unit has exponentially many counterfactuals relative to what is observable, modeling assumptions are necessary to relate unobserved potential outcomes to observed ones. We specify finite population models of potential outcomes through three distinct hierarchical components: an interference graph, an exposure mapping, and an outcome model. Such assumptions constrain the entries of 𝕋\mathbb{T} in two different ways. The interference graph and exposure mappings are exclusion restrictions. The interference graph specifies which treatment coordinates can enter a unit’s full-assignment potential outcome and the exposure mapping specifies how those coordinates aggregate. When combined, the interference graph and the exposure mapping partition the 2n2^{n} columns of 𝕋\mathbb{T} into equivalence classes for each row and require 𝕋\mathbb{T} to be constant within each class. On the other hand, Outcome models are a different kind of constraint: they do not merge columns of 𝕋\mathbb{T}, but instead impose functional constraints on the values 𝕋\mathbb{T} takes across distinct potential outcomes, potentially linking entries within a row or across rows (units). The classical no-interference setting is the most restrictive exclusion restriction, forcing each row to take only two distinct values across all 2n2^{n} columns. Formally, each exclusion restriction is specified by an equivalence relation ∼i\sim_{i} on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} that 𝕋\mathbb{T} must respect, meaning 𝐳∼i𝐳′⇒Yi(𝐳)=Yi(𝐳′)\mathbf{z}\sim_{i}\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\Rightarrow Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}); 𝕋\mathbb{T} is then fully determined by its values on the class representatives.

2.1 Interference graph

The first restriction specifies the set of units in the finite popluation whose treatment assignments effect Yi​(𝐳)Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}).

Assumption 1 (Interference exclusion restriction).

For each unit ii, there exists a subset Ni⊆{1,…,n}∖{i}N_{i}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\} such that, for any two treatment allocations 𝐳\mathbf{z} and 𝐳′\mathbf{z}^{\prime},

zi=zi′andzNi=zNi′⟹Yi​(𝐳)=Yi​(𝐳′).z_{i}=z_{i}^{\prime}\quad\text{and}\quad z_{N_{i}}=z^{\prime}_{N_{i}}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}).

Formally, Assumption 1 is the equivalence relation

𝐳∼iG𝐳′⇔zi=zi′ and 𝐳Ni=𝐳′Ni,\mathbf{z}\sim_{i}^{G}\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\;\iff\;z_{i}=z_{i}^{\prime}\text{ and }\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}=\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}},

which partitions {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} into 2di+12^{d_{i}+1} equivalence classes for row ii, where di=|Ni|d_{i}=|N_{i}|. Row ii of 𝕋\mathbb{T} takes at most 2di+12^{d_{i}+1} distinct values—one per class—and the potential outcome can be written as

Yi​(𝐳):=Yi​(zi,𝐳Ni),Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}):=Y_{i}(z_{i},\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}), (2.1)

depending only on ii’s own treatment and the treatments of units in NiN_{i}. The neighborhoods {Ni}i=1n\{N_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} may overlap, be asymmetric, or vary in size across units. For a fixed Table of Science, there is a minimal neighborhood

Ni⋆={j≠i:∃𝐳,𝐳′ differing only in zj such that Yi(𝐳)≠Yi(𝐳′)}.N_{i}^{\star}=\left\{j\neq i:\exists\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\text{ differing only in }z_{j}\text{ such that }Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})\neq Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime})\right\}.

The collection {Ni⋆}\{N_{i}^{\star}\} can be encoded via a minimal functional interference graph G⋆=(V,E⋆)G^{\star}=(V,E^{\star}) on nn nodes. The vertices of the graph VV correspond to the nn units in the finite population. A directed edge from node jj to node ii exists if the treatment of unit jj can affect the potential outcome of unit ii. In the remainder of the paper, we work with a specified interference graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and the corresponding neighborhoods {Ni}i=1n\{N_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}, under Assumption 1. Issues arising from random or misspecified interference graphs are discussed in the remark below. We use the degree to denote the in-degree of this graph GG. Setting Ni={1,…,n}∖{i}N_{i}=\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus\{i\} recovers the complete interference case in which all 2n2^{n} entries of each row of 𝕋\mathbb{T} are distinct (the restriction is vacuous), while Ni=∅N_{i}=\emptyset yields the classical SUTVA case in which each row takes only two distinct values.

It is useful to distinguish the interference graph from an observed social graph. The interference graph is an abstract representation of restrictions on the potential-outcome table. It may or may not coincide with a social graph, be an induced subgraph of it, or be a complete graph with the strength of interference modeled through an exposure function. In social-network settings, a natural choice is to set NiN_{i} to ii’s neighbors in the social graph (one-hop interference), or to all units within graph distance kk (multi-hop interference). Partial interference, where units can be partitioned into disjoint groups and interference is assumed to occur only within groups, is another special case (Sobel, 2006; Hudgens and Halloran, 2008). Spatial and bipartite interference models can also be represented by appropriate choices of GG; see Appendix A.

Remark 0 (Random and misspecified interference).

The minimal functional interference graph G⋆G^{\star} may not be known in applications, and the specified interference graph GG may itself be noisy or random. The graph GG used in analysis should therefore be understood as an assumed interference graph. If the assumed interference neighborhoods NiN_{i} satisfies Ni⋆⊆NiN_{i}^{\star}\subseteq N_{i}, the exclusion restriction remains valid but the representation is nonminimal. If, on the other hand, NiN_{i} omits units in Ni⋆N_{i}^{\star}, the interference graph is misspecified. Another approach is to treat the interference graph as random, and model the observed graph using a distribution; see Bhattacharya et al. (2020), Li and Wager (2022), and Ohnishi et al. (2025) for examples. For doubly robust estimators under a misspecified GG, see Weinstein and Nevo (2026).

Dependence graphs

The interference graph should not be confused with the dependence graph used in large-sample analysis of design based estimators. The interference graph is a restriction on the arguments of the potential-outcomes. A dependence graph is a probabilistic object attached to a particular collection of random variables, such as observed outcomes or estimator summands. Under independent Bernoulli assignment, this dependence may be induced by overlapping interference neighborhoods. Under dependent randomization designs, such as complete or cluster randomization, the assignment mechanism can induce additional dependence even when the interference neighborhoods do not overlap. We define the dependence graph formally in Section 4.1, where it is used for variance and consistency results.

Under Assumption 1, row ii of 𝕋\mathbb{T} takes at most 2di+12^{d_{i}+1} distinct values; 𝕋\mathbb{T} itself remains an n×2nn\times 2^{n} table, but is fully determined by specifying these 2di+12^{d_{i}+1} values per row. Even so, 2di+12^{d_{i}+1} can still be large; the exposure mapping, introduced next, provides a further exclusion restriction.

2.2 Exposure mapping

An exposure mapping (Aronow and Samii, 2017) summarizes neighborhood assignments into an exposure value,

ei=fi​(𝐳Ni)∈ℰi.e_{i}=f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})\in\mathcal{E}_{i}. (2.2)
Assumption 2 (Exposure mapping).

For each unit ii, there exists an exposure mapping fi:{0,1}|Ni|→ℰif_{i}:\{0,1\}^{|N_{i}|}\to\mathcal{E}_{i} such that, for any two neighborhood assignments 𝐳Ni\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}} and 𝐳Ni′\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}},

fi​(𝐳Ni)=fi​(𝐳Ni′)⟹Yi​(zi,𝐳Ni)=Yi​(zi,𝐳Ni′)for ​zi∈{0,1}.f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=f_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Y_{i}(z_{i},\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=Y_{i}(z_{i},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}})\quad\text{for }z_{i}\in\{0,1\}.

Formally, Assumption 2 is the equivalence relation

𝐳Ni∼if𝐳Ni′⇔fi(𝐳Ni)=fi(𝐳Ni′),\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}\sim_{i}^{f}\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}}\;\iff\;f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=f_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}}),

which coarsens ∼iG\sim_{i}^{G} by merging neighborhood assignments that produce the same exposure value. The function fif_{i} encodes how the treatment assignments of unit’s in NiN_{i} affect unit ii’s potential outcome. In the main text, we focus on the case where exposure values are one-dimensional and discrete, with |ℰi|=Ki|\mathcal{E}_{i}|=K_{i} exposure levels. Vector-valued and continuous exposures are discussed in Appendix A. We use the symbols ei=0e_{i}=0 to denote no exposure and ei=1e_{i}=1 to denote full exposure, with the exposure mapping specifying what these labels mean in context.

Combined, Assumptions 1 and 2 define the relation

𝐳∼i𝐳′⇔zi=zi′ and fi(𝐳Ni)=fi(𝐳Ni′),\mathbf{z}\sim_{i}\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\;\iff\;z_{i}=z_{i}^{\prime}\text{ and }f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=f_{i}(\mathbf{z}^{\prime}_{N_{i}}),

with 2​Ki2K_{i} equivalence classes, where Ki=|ℰi|K_{i}=|\mathcal{E}_{i}|. Row ii of 𝕋\mathbb{T} is thus fully determined by its 2​Ki2K_{i} values Yi​(zi,ei)Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i}), one for each (zi,ei)(z_{i},e_{i}) pair. We call each such value a reduced potential outcome. The collection of these distinct reduced potential outcomes,

𝕊={Yi(z,e):z∈{0,1},e∈ℰi,i=1,…,n},\mathbb{S}=\{Y_{i}(z,e):z\in\{0,1\},\ e\in\mathcal{E}_{i},\ i=1,\ldots,n\},

is the causal response surface induced by the specified interference neighborhoods and exposure mappings. Thus Yi​(𝐳)Y_{i}(\mathbf{z}) denotes a full-assignment potential outcome in 𝕋\mathbb{T}, whereas Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e) denotes the corresponding reduced potential outcome in 𝕊\mathbb{S}. When there is no interference, Yi​(z)Y_{i}(z) is the classical own-treatment potential outcome, the special case with no exposure argument. The non-parametric case corresponds to the identity mapping ei=𝐳Nie_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}, giving Ki=2diK_{i}=2^{d_{i}} and recovering ∼iG\sim_{i}^{G}.

Common examples of exposure mappings include symmetric or anonymous exposure, where fif_{i} depends only on the number or fraction of treated neighbors (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Manski, 2013); binary exposure, where ℰi={0,1}\mathcal{E}_{i}=\{0,1\}; additive exposure of the form fi​(𝐳Ni)=∑j∈Nihj​(zj)f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}h_{j}(z_{j}); and weighted or non-anonymous exposure, where fif_{i} incorporates neighbor identity, covariates, or graph distance.

2.3 A non-parametric decomposition of the causal response surface

Assumption 1 concerns who can interfere with unit ii, Assumption 2 concerns the form of that interference. Under Assumptions 1 and 2, 𝕋\mathbb{T} is fully determined by the causal response surface 𝕊\mathbb{S}, comprising 2​∑iKi2\sum_{i}K_{i} values. This response surface admits a natural non-parametric linear representation. This representation is an identity, and, without loss of generality, decomposes the potential outcome of each unit into three components: (a) a component depending only on a unit’s own treatment, (b) a component depending only on a unit’s exposure, and (c) the interaction between (a) and (b).

Theorem 2 (Non-parametric decomposition).

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, there exist functions Ai​(z)A_{i}(z), Bi​(ei)B_{i}(e_{i}) and Ci​(ei)C_{i}(e_{i}) such that, for each unit ii and each (zi,ei)∈{0,1}×ℰi(z_{i},e_{i})\in\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{E}_{i}, a potential outcome Yi​(z,e)∈𝕊Y_{i}(z,e)\in\mathbb{S} can be written as

Yi​(zi,ei)=Ai​(zi)+Bi​(ei)+zi​Ci​(ei)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(ei)+zi​Ci​(ei),Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i})=A_{i}(z_{i})+B_{i}(e_{i})+z_{i}C_{i}(e_{i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(e_{i})+z_{i}C_{i}(e_{i}), (2.3)

with the normalization Bi​(0)=Ci​(0)=0B_{i}(0)=C_{i}(0)=0.

The decomposition has a nice interpretation: the AiA_{i} term captures the part of the potential outcome depending only on unit ii’s own treatment, BiB_{i} term caputres the additive exposure component, and CiC_{i} the interaction between own-treatment and exposure (synergy or competition). These components define the corresponding direct, spillover, and interaction causal effects studied in Section 3.

The representation is a full-rank reparameterization of the causal response surface. In particular, it makes no assumptions on the potential outcomes and parametrizes the 2​Ki2K_{i} distinct values of row ii using 2​Ki2K_{i} linearly independent parameters. For example, under the identity exposure mapping, the number of exposure levels is Ki=2diK_{i}=2^{d_{i}} and the number of parameters in the representation Yi​(𝐳)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(zNi)+zi​Ci​(zNi)Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(z_{N_{i}})+z_{i}C_{i}(z_{N_{i}}) for each unit ii is 2di+12^{d_{i}+1}. Similarly, under arbitrary interference, Ki=2n−1K_{i}=2^{n-1} and Theorem 2 gives the non-parametric model Yi​(𝐳)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(𝐳−i)+zi​Ci​(𝐳−i)Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{-i})+z_{i}C_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{-i}), which has 2n2^{n} parameters for unit ii.

2.4 Outcome model

An outcome model imposes functional constraints on the 2​Ki2K_{i} distinct values of the causal response surface via specifying semi-parametric or parametric restrictions on {Ai,Bi,Ci}\{A_{i},B_{i},C_{i}\} in the decomposition (2.3); it does not operate by further merging assignment columns of 𝕋\mathbb{T}. Such constraints reduce the number of free parameters and may arise from scientific knowledge (e.g., a linear response) or be used to express sharp null hypotheses. Unlike exclusion restrictions, which operate within a single row of 𝕋\mathbb{T} before forming 𝕊\mathbb{S}, outcome models constrain the distinct potential outcomes of 𝕊\mathbb{S} and can also link entries across rows — homogeneity assumptions, for instance, require βi\beta_{i} to be common across units.

Additive effects.

A natural and commonly used restriction is that the direct and indirect effects enter additively, without interaction. In terms of the decomposition in (2.3), this corresponds to

Ci​(e)=0for all ​i​ and all ​e∈ℰi.C_{i}(e)=0\quad\text{for all }i\text{ and all }e\in\mathcal{E}_{i}.

The potential outcomes then simplify to Yi​(z,e)=Ai​(z)+Bi​(e)Y_{i}(z,e)=A_{i}(z)+B_{i}(e), and each unit has Ki+2K_{i}+2 free parameters instead of 2​Ki2K_{i}.

Constant (homogeneous) effects.

In some settings, it may be reasonable to assume that treatment and exposure effects do not vary across units. This can be written as

Ai(z)=A(z),Bi(e)=B(e),Ci(e)=C(e),for all i.A_{i}(z)=A(z),\qquad B_{i}(e)=B(e),\qquad C_{i}(e)=C(e),\quad\text{for all }i.

This links entries across rows of 𝕋\mathbb{T}: potential outcomes from different units are constrained to share the same effect functions, reducing the parameter count from O⁡(n​Ki)O(nK_{i}) to O⁡(K)O(K).

Linear effects in exposure.

When exposure levels are ordered (e.g., counts of treated neighbors), it may be plausible that the interference effect depends linearly on ee. One simple example is

Bi​(e)=γi​e,Ci​(e)=θi​e,B_{i}(e)=\gamma_{i}\,e,\qquad C_{i}(e)=\theta_{i}\,e,

which yields Yi​(z,e)=αi+βi​zi+γi​e+θi​z​eY_{i}(z,e)=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+\gamma_{i}e+\theta_{i}ze. If αi,βi,γi\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},\gamma_{i} and θi\theta_{i} are further assumed constant across units, the model reduces to a four-parameter linear dose-response formulation.

Sharp null hypotheses.

Outcome models can also be used to express sharp null hypotheses for randomization testing. The linear decomposition allows these to be stated precisely. For instance, a sharp null of no treatment effect under interference is

βi=0​ and ​Bi​(ei)=Ci​(ei)=0​ for all ​ei,i\beta_{i}=0\mbox{ and }B_{i}(e_{i})=C_{i}(e_{i})=0\mbox{ for all }e_{i},i

Similarly, the condition

Yi​(1,e)=Yi​(0,e)for all ​i​ and all ​e∈ℰi,Y_{i}(1,e)=Y_{i}(0,e)\quad\text{for all }i\text{ and all }e\in\mathcal{E}_{i},

is equivalent to the hypothesis Ai​(1)+Ci​(ei)=Ai​(0)A_{i}(1)+C_{i}(e_{i})=A_{i}(0) and implies sharp null of no treatment effect only under additivity (i.e. Ci​(ei)=0C_{i}(e_{i})=0). More targeted nulls, such as absence of spillover effects or no interaction effects, can be expressed by setting subsets of {Bi​(e),Ci​(e)}\{B_{i}(e),C_{i}(e)\} to zero. See Rosenbaum (2007); Aronow (2012); Pouget-Abadie et al. (2019); Athey et al. (2018); Basse et al. (2019); Puelz et al. (2022); Rigdon and Hudgens (2015) for construction of statistical tests under various such hypotheses.

Relation to estimation.

Outcome modeling assumptions are not required to define causal estimands. However, they can be used for model-assisted design and estimation. In the absence of such assumptions, the parameters {Ai,Bi,Ci}\{A_{i},B_{i},C_{i}\} vary freely across units and exposure levels. Imposing them constrains these parameters, so that a response observed under one treatment-exposure combination can inform missing responses under other combinations. If correctly specified, this model-assisted approach can significantly reduce variance at either the design or analysis stage.

2.5 Canonical model classes

Different choices of the interference neighborhood NiN_{i}, the exposure mapping fif_{i}, and the outcome model restrictions imposed on (Ai,Bi,Ci)(A_{i},B_{i},C_{i}) lead to different potential-outcome models. The decomposition in Theorem 2 encompasses the full range of models used in the literature. A non-parametric model imposes no restrictions on AiA_{i}, BiB_{i}, CiC_{i} beyond the interference neighborhood and exposure mapping; the functions themselves are unrestricted. A semi-parametric model imposes qualitative restrictions on AiA_{i}, BiB_{i}, CiC_{i}—such as additivity (Ci≡0C_{i}\equiv 0), symmetry, or monotonicity. A parametric model specifies finite-dimensional functional forms for AiA_{i}, BiB_{i}, CiC_{i}, for example linear functions of exposure or homogeneous effects across units. We present some commonly used examples below.

Example 3 (Arbitrary interference).

Let Ni={1,…,n}∖{i}N_{i}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\}, and let fi​(𝐳Ni)=𝐳Nif_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}. Then

Yi​(𝐳)=Yi​(zi,𝐳−i)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(𝐳−i)+zi​Ci​(𝐳−i).Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=Y_{i}(z_{i},\mathbf{z}_{-i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{-i})+z_{i}C_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{-i}).

Row ii of 𝕋\mathbb{T} takes 2n2^{n} distinct values; Assumption 1 places no constraint.

Example 4 (Neighborhood interference).

Let Ni⊊{1,…,n}∖{i}N_{i}\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\} be a specified proper subset, and let fi​(𝐳Ni)=𝐳Nif_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}. Then

Yi​(𝐳)=Yi​(zi,𝐳Ni)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(𝐳Ni)+zi​Ci​(𝐳Ni).Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=Y_{i}(z_{i},\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})+z_{i}C_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}}).

Row ii of 𝕋\mathbb{T} takes 2di+12^{d_{i}+1} distinct values, where di=|Ni|d_{i}=|N_{i}|; the exponent reduces from n−1n-1 to the local neighborhood size.

Example 5 (No interference).

Let Ni=∅N_{i}=\emptyset. Then Yi​(𝐳)=Yi​(zi)Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})=Y_{i}(z_{i}), which is the classical no-interference case. Each unit has two own-treatment potential outcomes.

Example 6 (Count or fractional exposure mappings).

Let ei=fi​(𝐳Ni)=∑j∈Nizje_{i}=f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j} denote the number of treated neighbors of unit ii, or alternatively let ei=∑j∈Nizj/die_{i}=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}/d_{i} denote the proportion of treated neighbors of unit ii. Then

Yi​(zi,ei)\displaystyle Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i}) =αi+βi​zi+Bi​(ei)+zi​Ci​(ei),\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(e_{i})+z_{i}C_{i}(e_{i}), (2.4)

where ei∈{0,1,…,di}e_{i}\in\{0,1,\ldots,d_{i}\} in the count case and ei∈{0,1/di,2/di,…,1}e_{i}\in\{0,1/d_{i},2/d_{i},\ldots,1\} in the fractional case. Under this model, the number of free parameters per unit is 2​(di+1)2(d_{i}+1). If additivity is imposed, Ci​(ei)=0C_{i}(e_{i})=0 for all eie_{i}, and the number of free parameters per unit reduces to di+2d_{i}+2.

Example 7 (Linear-in-means model).

Starting from equation (2.4), let Bi​(ei)=γi​eiB_{i}(e_{i})=\gamma_{i}e_{i} and Ci​(ei)=θi​eiC_{i}(e_{i})=\theta_{i}e_{i}. Then

Yi​(zi,ei)\displaystyle Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i}) =αi+βi​zi+γi​ei+θi​zi​ei.\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+\gamma_{i}e_{i}+\theta_{i}z_{i}e_{i}. (2.5)

If the interaction term is zero, the model becomes

Yi​(zi,ei)\displaystyle Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i}) =αi+βi​zi+γi​ei.\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+\gamma_{i}e_{i}. (2.6)

This additive linear outcome model is the linear-in-means model used in the econometrics literature (Manski, 1993; Bramoullé et al., 2009; Graham, 2008).

Example 8 (2×22\times 2 exposure mapping).

Let fi​(𝐳Ni)=0f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=0 if all elements of 𝐳Ni\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}} are 00 and fi​(𝐳Ni)=1f_{i}(\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}})=1 if at least one element of 𝐳Ni\mathbf{z}_{N_{i}} is 11. This gives the two-by-two response-surface model, or binary exposure mapping,

Yi​(zi,ei)=αi+βi​zi+γi​ei+θi​zi​ei,\displaystyle Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+\gamma_{i}e_{i}+\theta_{i}z_{i}e_{i}, (2.7)

where ei∈{0,1}e_{i}\in\{0,1\} and zi∈{0,1}z_{i}\in\{0,1\}. Each unit has four distinct potential outcomes. Setting θi=0\theta_{i}=0 gives the additive binary exposure mapping,

Yi​(zi,ei)=αi+βi​zi+γi​ei,\displaystyle Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+\gamma_{i}e_{i}, (2.8)

with three free parameters per unit.

Example 9 (Weighted exposure mappings).

In non-anonymous interference, the exposure depends on the identity or covariates of the neighbors. For example, one may specify

ei=∑j∈Niwi​j​zj,e_{i}=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}w_{ij}z_{j},

and then write

Yi​(zi,ei)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(ei)+zi​Ci​(ei).Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}(e_{i})+z_{i}C_{i}(e_{i}).

The additive version of this model has been used for total treatment effects under network interference (Yu et al., 2022). Additional non-anonymous and spatial examples are given in Appendix A.

The three canonical non-parametric representations—arbitrary interference, neighborhood interference, and exposure mapping (illustrated by examples 4–7 above)—are compared in Section 4 with respect to their estimation bottlenecks.

3 Defining causal estimands under network interference

Under treatment interference, there are many non-equivalent ways to define causal effects, and the appropriate estimand depends on the scientific question of interest. Causal estimands in the framework of Section 2 are summaries of the causal response surface Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e). We study two broad classes: average causal effects (ACEs), which are contrasts of fixed potential outcomes and do not involve any distribution over treatment allocations; and expected causal effects (ECEs), which are contrasts of expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy.

3.1 Average causal effects under network interference

Average causal effects (ACEs) are defined as contrasts between two fixed potential outcomes. Once an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping have been specified, the treatment–exposure space for unit ii is

𝒳i={0,1}×ℰi.\mathcal{X}_{i}=\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{E}_{i}.

For an assignment 𝐳\mathbf{z}, let

Di​(𝐳)=(zi,ei​(𝐳))∈𝒳iD_{i}(\mathbf{z})=(z_{i},e_{i}(\mathbf{z}))\in\mathcal{X}_{i}

denote the treatment–exposure combination realized by unit ii. A generic ACE compares two fixed treatment–exposure combinations

di+=(zi+,ei+),di−=(zi−,ei−),di+,di−∈𝒳i.d_{i}^{+}=(z_{i}^{+},e_{i}^{+}),\qquad d_{i}^{-}=(z_{i}^{-},e_{i}^{-}),\qquad d_{i}^{+},d_{i}^{-}\in\mathcal{X}_{i}.

Let d+={di+}i=1nd^{+}=\{d_{i}^{+}\}_{i=1}^{n} and d−={di−}i=1nd^{-}=\{d_{i}^{-}\}_{i=1}^{n}. The corresponding ACE is defined as

τACE​(d+,d−)=1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(di+)−Yi​(di−)).\tau_{\mathrm{ACE}}(d^{+},d^{-})\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}(d_{i}^{+})-Y_{i}(d_{i}^{-})\Big). (3.1)

This definition directly generalizes the average treatment effect under no-interference assumptions, and does not require assumptions on the functional form of the response surface. Different choices of di+d_{i}^{+} and di−d_{i}^{-} correspond to different causal questions about treatment and interference.

This definition also includes arbitrary interference as a special case: take Ni={1,…,n}∖{i}N_{i}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\} and use the identity exposure mapping ei=𝐳−ie_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{-i}. Then Di​(𝐳)=(zi,𝐳−i)D_{i}(\mathbf{z})=(z_{i},\mathbf{z}_{-i}), and equation (3.1) defines ACEs directly in terms of the full treatment vector.

We now give a few examples of ACEs. Recall that the exposure levels ei=0e_{i}=0 and ei=1e_{i}=1 are special values defined to represent the situations when a unit is not exposed or fully exposed respectively.

Direct treatment effect.

The direct treatment effect compares the average outcome under treatment versus control when exposure is held at the baseline level of 00:

τDTE=τACE​(d+,d−)=1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(1,0)−Yi​(0,0)).\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}\,=\,\tau_{\mathrm{ACE}}(d^{+},d^{-})\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}(1,0)-Y_{i}(0,0)\Big). (3.2)

where di+=(1,0)d_{i}^{+}=(1,0) and di−=(0,0)d_{i}^{-}=(0,0) for all ii. The direct treatment effect is the interference analogue of the average treatment effect in the no-interference case. It measures the average effect of treatment on a unit when the exposure is fixed at the baseline level.

Average indirect effects.

For two exposure levels ea,eb∈ℰe_{a},e_{b}\in\mathcal{E} and own treatment z∈{0,1}z\in\{0,1\}, define the average indirect effect

τIE​(z,ea,eb)=1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(z,eb)−Yi​(z,ea)),\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(z;e_{a},e_{b})\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}(z,e_{b})-Y_{i}(z,e_{a})\Big), (3.3)

which holds the unit’s own treatment fixed and varies only the exposure regime between the two levels. The pair (ea,eb)(e_{a},e_{b}) is part of the estimand: spillover questions can concern any two exposure levels, and the baseline eae_{a} need not be the no-exposure level. The special case ea=0e_{a}=0 recovers the level-specific indirect effects τIEC​(e)=τIE​(0,0,e)\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}(e)=\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(0;0,e) and τIET​(e)=τIE​(1,0,e)\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}(e)=\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(1;0,e) on control and treated units, respectively. Writing τIEC=τIEC​(ei𝟏)\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}=\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}(e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}) and τIET=τIET​(ei𝟏)\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}=\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}(e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}) for the full-exposure versions at the all-treated level e=ei𝟏e=e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}},

τIEC=1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(0,1)−Yi​(0,0)),\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}(0,1)-Y_{i}(0,0)\Big), (3.4)
τIET=1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(1,1)−Yi​(1,0)).\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}(1,1)-Y_{i}(1,0)\Big). (3.5)

A natural two-level exposure pair arises from the any-treated exposure map

Ui=𝟙{∑j∈NiZj≥1},U_{i}=\mathds{1}\Big\{\textstyle\sum_{j\in N_{i}}Z_{j}\geq 1\Big\}, (3.6)

which records whether at least one neighbor of unit ii is treated. With ea=0e_{a}=0 and eb=1e_{b}=1, the contrast τIE​(z,0,1)\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(z;0,1) measures the average effect of moving a unit with own treatment zz from an environment free of treated neighbors to one with at least one treated neighbor. Held at z=0z=0, this is the influencer spillover effect estimated in influencer-seeding experiments in social-network settings: the effect on an average untreated unit of the presence of a treated influencer among its neighbors (Paluck et al., 2016; Aral and Walker, 2012; Bond et al., 2012). Section 5.3 shows that this two-level estimand is estimable at constant-order focal propensities on bounded-degree graphs by a sparse-seeding design, in contrast to the exponentially small propensities of its extreme full-exposure special cases.

By Proposition 12 below, τIE​(0,ea,eb)=n−1​∑i{Bi​(eb)−Bi​(ea)}\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(0;e_{a},e_{b})=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\{B_{i}(e_{b})-B_{i}(e_{a})\} captures the additive exposure component, while τIE​(1,ea,eb)\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(1;e_{a},e_{b}) adds the treatment–exposure interaction; the two coincide under additivity (Ci≡0C_{i}\equiv 0).

Remark 0.

We use the term average indirect effect for the fixed-exposure ACE estimands above. This is different from the average indirect effect introduced in Hu et al. (2022), which we define as the expected indirect effect as it belongs to the expected causal effects class.

Total treatment effect.

The total treatment effect compares the fully treated and fully exposed condition to the fully untreated and unexposed condition:

τTTE=τACE​(d+,d−)=1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(1,1)−Yi​(0,0)).\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}\,=\,\tau_{\mathrm{ACE}}(d^{+},d^{-})\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(Y_{i}(1,1)-Y_{i}(0,0)\Big). (3.7)

where di+=(1,1)d_{i}^{+}=(1,1) and di−=(0,0)d_{i}^{-}=(0,0) for all ii.

3.2 Expected causal effects under network interference

Average causal effects compare two fixed potential outcomes. In many cases, however, the exposure of a unit is random under a policy of scientific interest. Expected causal effects are defined as contrasts of allocation-averaged responses, where entries of the causal response surface are averaged over one or more allocation distributions specified by the estimand. The target allocation policy is part of the causal question itself. A generic expected causal effect contrasts random treatment–exposure combinations induced by an allocation policy. Let 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} and 𝒬−\mathcal{Q}^{-} denote two allocation policies. For each unit ii, let

Di+​(𝐙),Di−​(𝐙)D_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}),\qquad D_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})

be two corresponding random elements of 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i}. A generic ECE is any contrast of the form

τECE​(D+,D−,𝒬+,𝒬−)=1n​∑i=1n[𝔼𝒬+​Yi​{Di+​(𝐙)}−𝔼𝒬−​Yi​{Di−​(𝐙)}].\tau_{\mathrm{ECE}}(D^{+},D^{-};\mathcal{Q}^{+},\mathcal{Q}^{-})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}^{+}}Y_{i}\{D_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})\}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}^{-}}Y_{i}\{D_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})\}\right]. (3.8)

The distributions 𝒬+,𝒬−\mathcal{Q}^{+},\mathcal{Q}^{-} can be different from the experimental design PP, but are often induced by PP. For example, a study may use a randomized saturation design with several treatment probabilities to estimate the expected effect of a single target rollout policy, such as treating 70 percent of units; the rollout policy defines the estimand, while the saturation design is chosen to provide overlap and precision. For the special case where 𝒬+=𝒬−=𝒬\mathcal{Q}^{+}=\mathcal{Q}^{-}=\mathcal{Q}, we write τECE​(D+,D−,𝒬)\tau_{\mathrm{ECE}}(D^{+},D^{-};\mathcal{Q}). We now consider some examples of expected causal effects used in the literature. Let P𝒬​(Ei=e)P_{\mathcal{Q}}(E_{i}=e) denote the marginal distribution of the exposure level EiE_{i} under allocation policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The expected response of unit ii under own treatment z∈{0,1}z\in\{0,1\} is

μi​(z,𝒬)=∑e∈ℰYi​(z,e)​P𝒬​(Ei=e).\mu_{i}(z;\mathcal{Q})\,=\,\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}Y_{i}(z,e)\,P_{\mathcal{Q}}(E_{i}=e). (3.9)

Expected (average) direct effect.

The expected direct effect compares the average outcome under treatment versus control, averaging over the exposure distribution induced by the allocation policy:

τEDE​(𝒬)=𝔼𝒬​[1n​∑i=1n(Yi​(1,Ei)−Yi​(0,Ei))]=1n​∑i=1n(μi​(1,𝒬)−μi​(0,𝒬)).\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(Y_{i}(1,E_{i})-Y_{i}(0,E_{i})\right)\right]\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big(\mu_{i}(1;\mathcal{Q})-\mu_{i}(0;\mathcal{Q})\Big). (3.10)

This is the one-contrast special case of (3.8) with Di+​(𝐙)=(1,Ei)D_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})=(1,E_{i}), Di−​(𝐙)=(0,Ei)D_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})=(0,E_{i}), and common policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. The expected average direct effect is also known as the Average Direct Effect (ADE) in the literature, see Sävje et al. (2017). We use the term expected direct effect to emphasize that it is an ECE and not an ACE.

Expected (average) indirect effect.

The expected indirect effect compares the expected outcome of unit ii when unit jj’s treatment is changed, keeping all other treatment assignments the same. For j∈Nij\in N_{i}, define

Ei+j=fi​(𝐙Ni∖{j},Zj=1),Ei−j=fi​(𝐙Ni∖{j},Zj=0),E_{i}^{+j}=f_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}\setminus\{j\}},Z_{j}=1),\qquad E_{i}^{-j}=f_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}\setminus\{j\}},Z_{j}=0),

as the exposure of unit ii when neighbor jj is treated or untreated, holding all others fixed. Then,

τEIE(𝒬)=1n∑i=1n∑j∈Ni𝔼𝒬[Yi(Zi,Ei+j))−Yi(Zi,Ei−j)].\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}\!\Big[Y_{i}\!\big(Z_{i},E_{i}^{+j})\big)-Y_{i}\!\big(Z_{i},E_{i}^{-j}\big)\Big]. (3.11)

This is an aggregation of neighbor-specific ECE contrasts. For each ordered pair (i,j)(i,j) with j∈Nij\in N_{i}, define

Di​j+​(𝐙)=(Zi,Ei+j),Di​j−​(𝐙)=(Zi,Ei−j).D_{ij}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})=(Z_{i},E_{i}^{+j}),\qquad D_{ij}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})=(Z_{i},E_{i}^{-j}).

The expected indirect effect is also known as the Average Indirect Effect. The arbitrary interference version of this estimand was introduced in Hu et al. (2022).

Proposition 11 (Policy derivative representation).

Under a Bernoulli policy 𝒬π\mathcal{Q}_{\pi} with 𝐙∼∏iBern⁡(πi)\mathbf{Z}\sim\prod_{i}\mathrm{Bern}(\pi_{i}), writing μ⁡(π)=n−1​∑i𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei​(𝐙Ni))]\mu(\pi)=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}}))] for the expected population outcome, the total policy derivative τTPE​(π)=∑j∂μ⁡(π)/∂πj\tau_{\mathrm{TPE}}(\pi)=\sum_{j}\partial\mu(\pi)/\partial\pi_{j} decomposes as τTPE​(π)=τEDE​(π)+τEIE​(π)\tau_{\mathrm{TPE}}(\pi)=\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\pi)+\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi), recovering the Average Direct Effect / Average Indirect Effect decomposition of Hu et al. (2022) under arbitrary interference as a special case. Under symmetric exposure mappings, EIE has a simpler finite-difference form; details are in Appendix C.6.

Expected policy effect.

The general definition also allows the two arms of the contrast to be averaged under different allocation policies. Let 𝒬+\mathcal{Q}^{+} and 𝒬−\mathcal{Q}^{-} be two policies, for example Bernoulli policies with treatment probabilities p+p_{+} and p−p_{-}. The expected policy effect is

τpolicy​(𝒬+,𝒬−)=1n​∑i=1n[𝔼𝒬+​Yi​{Di​(𝐙)}−𝔼𝒬−​Yi​{Di​(𝐙)}].\tau_{\mathrm{policy}}(\mathcal{Q}^{+},\mathcal{Q}^{-})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}^{+}}Y_{i}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}^{-}}Y_{i}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}\right]. (3.12)

This is the special case of (3.8) with Di+​(𝐙)=Di−​(𝐙)=Di​(𝐙)D_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})=D_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})=D_{i}(\mathbf{Z}), but with 𝒬+≠𝒬−\mathcal{Q}^{+}\neq\mathcal{Q}^{-}. It represents questions such as comparing an allocation policy with 50 percent treatment probability to one with 20 percent treatment probability.

Mixed effects that combine policy-averaged and fixed-baseline potential outcomes (EIC, EIT, ETE) are defined in Appendix C.1.

3.3 Algebraic representation of ACEs and ECEs

We now represent the two classes of estimands using the non-parametric linear decomposition of the causal response surface.

Proposition 12 (Representation of fixed and expected effects).

Under the non-parametric linear decomposition of Theorem 2,

Yi​(z,e)=αi+βi​z+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e),Bi​(0)=Ci​(0)=0,Y_{i}(z,e)=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e),\qquad B_{i}(0)=C_{i}(0)=0,

the average causal effects can be written as

τDTE\displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}} =1n​∑iβi,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i},
τIE​(z,ea,eb)\displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(z;e_{a},e_{b}) =1n​∑i{Bi​(eb)−Bi​(ea)+z⁡(Ci​(eb)−Ci​(ea))},\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{B_{i}(e_{b})-B_{i}(e_{a})+z\,(C_{i}(e_{b})-C_{i}(e_{a}))\},
τIEC​(e)\displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}(e) =1n​∑iBi​(e),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}B_{i}(e),
τIET​(e)\displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}(e) =1n​∑i{Bi​(e)+Ci​(e)},\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{B_{i}(e)+C_{i}(e)\},
τTTE\displaystyle\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}} =1n​∑i{βi+Bi​(1)+Ci​(1)}.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{\beta_{i}+B_{i}(1)+C_{i}(1)\}.

For an allocation policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, let B¯𝒬=n−1​∑i𝔼𝒬​[Bi​(Ei)]\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[B_{i}(E_{i})] and C¯𝒬=n−1​∑i𝔼𝒬​[Ci​(Ei)]\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[C_{i}(E_{i})]. Then

τEDE​(𝒬)=1n​∑iβi+C¯𝒬.\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

The mixed effects EIC, EIT, and ETE satisfy analogous expressions: τEIC​(𝒬)=B¯𝒬\tau_{\mathrm{EIC}}(\mathcal{Q})=\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}}, τEIT​(𝒬)=B¯𝒬+C¯𝒬\tau_{\mathrm{EIT}}(\mathcal{Q})=\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}}+\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}, and τETE​(𝒬)=n−1​∑iβi+B¯𝒬+C¯𝒬\tau_{\mathrm{ETE}}(\mathcal{Q})=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}}+\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}; see Appendix C.1.

These representations connect the estimands directly to the components of the non-parametric response-surface decomposition. While fixed-exposure ACEs select values of BiB_{i} and CiC_{i} at specific exposure levels, ECEs average these same components over the exposure distribution induced by the allocation policy. Specifically, τDTE\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}} isolates the direct effect component βi\beta_{i}, whereas τIEC\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}} and τIET\tau_{\mathrm{IET}} capture the pure indirect and indirect-plus-interference components, respectively. Notably, the expected direct effect encapsulates both the pure direct component and the treatment–interference interaction component, the latter being 00 under additivity. This yields the following corollary:

Corollary 13.

Under additivity of the causal response surface, τEDE​(𝒬)=τDTE\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}} for every allocation policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Without additivity, the expected direct effect contains the policy-weighted interaction component C¯𝒬\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}} and is policy-dependent: estimators that target EDE do not target the fixed-exposure DTE. The total treatment effect also has a decomposition:

Proposition 14 (ACE total effect decomposition).

The total treatment effect decomposes as

τTTE=τDTE+τIET.\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}.

Under additivity (Ci≡0C_{i}\equiv 0), τIET=τIEC\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}=\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}, so τTTE=τDTE+τIEC\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}.

Decompositions involving the mixed effects EIC, EIT, and ETE are given in Appendix C.1.

3.4 Relevant and Nuisance Potential Outcomes

Another distinction between average causal effects (ACEs) and expected causal effects (ECEs) ties to which entries of 𝕊\mathbb{S} define the estimand. In a non-parametric framework, no outcome model is imposed on the distinct potential outcomes: observing one element of 𝕊\mathbb{S} provides no information about another distinct element of 𝕊\mathbb{S}. Thus, potential outcomes that do not enter the definition of an estimand are uninformative for its non-parametric estimation, regardless of how often an experimental design reveals them. We formalize this distinction by partitioning the causal response surface relative to a target estimand.

Definition 15 (Relevant and nuisance potential outcomes).

Fix a causal estimand τ\tau, defined as a functional of the causal response surface 𝕊\mathbb{S}. A potential outcome Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e) is relevant for τ\tau if the functional defining τ\tau depends on Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e). The relevant set is

ℛτ={Yi​(z,e)∈𝕊:τ​ depends on ​Yi​(z,e)}.\mathcal{R}_{\tau}=\{Y_{i}(z,e)\in\mathbb{S}:\tau\text{ depends on }Y_{i}(z,e)\}.

The complement ℛτc=𝕊∖ℛτ\mathcal{R}_{\tau}^{c}=\mathbb{S}\setminus\mathcal{R}_{\tau} is the set of nuisance potential outcomes for τ\tau.

For ACEs, the relevant set ℛτ\mathcal{R}_{\tau} is typically a sparse subset of the causal response surface. For example, a direct treatment effect depends only on

{Yi​(1,0),Yi​(0,0)}i=1n,\{Y_{i}(1,0),Y_{i}(0,0)\}_{i=1}^{n},

whereas a total treatment effect depends only on

{Yi​(1,1),Yi​(0,0)}i=1n.\{Y_{i}(1,1),Y_{i}(0,0)\}_{i=1}^{n}.

All other entries of 𝕊\mathbb{S} are nuisance for non-parametric estimation of these estimands. For example, if a design exposes a unit to an intermediate exposure level ee, revealing Yi​(1,e)Y_{i}(1,e), that observation provides no non-parametric information about target potential outcomes such as Yi​(1,1)Y_{i}(1,1) or Yi​(1,0)Y_{i}(1,0). Without an outcome model relating distinct potential outcomes of 𝕊\mathbb{S} across treatment or exposure levels, observations from nuisance potential outcomes cannot reduce variance for the target estimand. They may instead waste probability mass, contribute bias, or require outcome modeling assumptions that go beyond non-parametric estimation.

For ECEs, the allocation policy is part of the definition of the estimand. Any treatment–exposure combination that is assigned positive probability under the allocation policy is included in the relevant set ℛτ\mathcal{R}_{\tau} of an ECE. For example, the relevant set for the expected direct effect τEDE​(𝒬)\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q}) is the set of Yi​(1,e)Y_{i}(1,e) and Yi​(0,e)Y_{i}(0,e) for each exposure level ee in the support of the exposure distribution induced by policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q}. When the policy induces positive probability on every treatment–exposure combination in the specified representation, the relevant set is the entire causal response surface.

This difference in relevant potential outcomes leads to different non-parametric estimation problems, as discussed in Section 4. For ACEs, the design must reveal the relevant potential outcomes. Non-parametric estimation thus requires the propensity scores for those combinations to be bounded away from zero. When the probability of revealing the relevant potential outcomes is rare under the design, inverse-probability weights become unstable and variance can be large. Consequently, non-parametric estimation of ACEs often requires specialized designs that place sufficient probability mass on the relevant potential outcomes; such designs are discussed in Section 6. For ECEs, the estimand instead averages over the treatment–exposure combinations induced by the policy. The relevant support is therefore determined by the policy itself. In this case, the main variance bottleneck is not the probability of observing a narrow set of fixed treatment–exposure entries, but the overlap between the observed assignment design and the policy. Importance-weighted HT estimators use outcomes across the support of the policy, with precision governed by policy-to-design weights, network dependence, and the extent of support overlap.

3.5 Conditional expected effects

The two classes introduced in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 also clarify conditional estimands that have appeared in the literature on partial interference. Hudgens and Halloran (2008) introduced causal effects under partial interference based on conditional expectations of potential outcomes. In their setting, units are partitioned into disjoint interference groups, and causal effects are defined by conditioning on the treatment assignment within the group. Formally, one considers conditional potential outcomes of the form

𝔼⁡[Yi​(z,e)|Zi=z],\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[Y_{i}(z,e)\,\big|\,Z_{i}=z\bigr],

where the expectation is taken with respect to the distribution of exposure in the group, conditional on the individual treatment. Estimands are then defined as contrasts between such conditional expectations. These estimands can be viewed as conditional expected causal effects, which differ from the marginal expected effects defined in Section 3.2. Conditional estimands depend on the randomization scheme within groups, and are most natural under two-stage designs with partial interference in which treatment probabilities are assigned at the group level. In arbitrary network interference, or under designs where a unit’s treatment and exposure are dependent, conditioning on ZiZ_{i} also changes the exposure distribution. The resulting estimand remains well defined, but its interpretation depends on the conditional allocation distribution; see Sävje et al. (2017) for a discussion.

4 Estimation of ACEs and ECEs

In this section, we study design-unbiased estimators of ACEs and ECEs. In particular, under a fixed experimental design PP, we derive upper bounds for the variance of canonical Horvitz–Thompson (HT) estimators as well as lower bounds on the design variance of any unbiased estimator. Finally, we establish the conditions under which these estimators achieve design consistency. Under a growing sequence of finite populations indexed by nn, an estimator τ^n\hat{\tau}_{n} is design-MSE consistent for τn\tau_{n} if

𝔼Pn​{(τ^n−τn)2}→0.\mathbb{E}_{P_{n}}\{(\hat{\tau}_{n}-\tau_{n})^{2}\}\to 0.

The estimation machinery applies to any choice of interference graph and exposure mapping. As examples, we study estimation under the three examples introduced in Section 2: arbitrary interference (Zi,𝐙−i)(Z_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{-i}), neighborhood interference (Zi,𝐙Ni)(Z_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}}), and exposure mappings (Zi,ei​(𝐙Ni))(Z_{i},e_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}})). Throughout this section, no outcome modeling assumptions are imposed. Once the interference neighborhood and exposure mapping have been fixed, non-parametric estimation treats the distinct potential outcomes of 𝕊\mathbb{S} as unrestricted. Observing one distinct potential outcome Yi​(z,e)Y_{i}(z,e) does not, without an outcome model, identify or reduce uncertainty about another distinct potential outcome Yi​(z′,e′)Y_{i}(z^{\prime},e^{\prime}).

4.1 Dependence from interference and design

Consider a generic estimator τ^n\hat{\tau}_{n} that is a function of random variables X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n}. In the design-based setting, the potential-outcome table is fixed, so any observed-outcome term Yio​b​s=Yi​(𝐙)Y_{i}^{obs}=Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) is a measurable function of the treatment assignment vector. Thus each XiX_{i} can be written generally as Xi=gi​(𝐙)X_{i}=g_{i}(\mathbf{Z}). The variance bounds in the sequel use dependence graphs for the random variables {Xi}\{X_{i}\}.

Definition 16 (Dependence graph and average dependence).

Consider random variables {Xi}i=1n\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}. A graph Gdep=(V,Edep)G_{\mathrm{dep}}=(V,E_{\mathrm{dep}}) is a dependence graph of {Xi}i=1n\{X_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} if the following holds: whenever two disjoint sets of vertices A,B⊆VA,B\subseteq V have no edge between them, the collections {Xi:i∈A}\{X_{i}:i\in A\} and {Xj:j∈B}\{X_{j}:j\in B\} are independent. We write ci​j=1c_{ij}=1 when ii and jj are adjacent in this dependence graph and ci​j=0c_{ij}=0 otherwise. The dependence degree of ii is

ci=∑j≠ici​j,c_{i}=\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij},

and the average dependence degree is

cavg=1n​∑i=1nci=1n​∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j.c_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}.
Remark 0 (Estimator dependence versus interference neighborhoods).

The dependence graph is an object associated with the estimator t^​a​un\hat{t}au_{n} and the random variables XiX_{i}, not directly with the causal estimand. If XiX_{i} depends only on a subvector of the treatment assignment, we may write Xi=gi​(𝐙Ai)X_{i}=g_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{A_{i}}), where Ai⊆{1,…,n}A_{i}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} is an assignment-dependence set for that estimator variable. The set AiA_{i} includes the treatment assignment coordinates used by the observed outcome and by any random weights or normalizing factors. When an interference graph with neighborhoods NiN_{i} is specified, write 𝒞i={i}∪Ni\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{i\}\cup N_{i} for the closed interference neighborhood; this includes arbitrary interference as the special case Ni={1,…,n}∖{i}N_{i}=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{i\}. For the local HT/IPW estimators below, the observed outcome has the form Yi​(Zi,𝐙Ni)Y_{i}(Z_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}}) and the weights are also a function of (Zi,𝐙Ni)(Z_{i},\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}}). Hence Ai⊆𝒞iA_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{i}. Ratio estimators such as Hajek estimators may introduce additional assignment dependence because their weights depend on the full treatment assignment vector 𝐙\mathbf{Z}.

Typically, the variables XiX_{i} and XjX_{j} can be dependent for two reasons: their treatment-assignment index sets AiA_{i} and AjA_{j} can overlap because of interference, and the randomization design can directly induce dependence among treatment assignments, even when AiA_{i} and AjA_{j} do not overlap. Below, we separate these two sources into interference-overlap dependence and residual design dependence.

Under independent treatment assignment, there is no residual design dependence. The remaining dependence is induced by overlap of the assignment coordinates on which the variables XiX_{i} depend: if Xi=gi​(𝐙Ai)X_{i}=g_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{A_{i}}), then 𝟙{Ai∩Aj≠∅}\mathds{1}\{A_{i}\cap A_{j}\neq\emptyset\} gives a valid dependence edge under independent assignment. The following lemma records the closed-neighborhood specialization used for the local HT/IPW estimators studied below.

Lemma 18 (Dependence induced by local estimator variables).

Suppose the treatment assignments are mutually independent and XiX_{i} is a function of 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}, where 𝒞i={i}∪Ni\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{i\}\cup N_{i} is the closed interference neighborhood of unit ii. Then a valid dependence graph of {Xi}\{X_{i}\} is obtained by setting

ci​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅},i≠j.c_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\},\qquad i\neq j.

If the interference graph is undirected, di=|Ni|d_{i}=|N_{i}|, and B2​(i)B_{2}(i) denotes the two-hop interference neighborhood of ii, including ii, then

ci=|B2​(i)|−1c_{i}=|B_{2}(i)|-1

and

b2,avg:=1n​∑i=1n{|B2​(i)|−1}=cavg,d¯≤b2,avg≤min⁡{n−1,1n​∑i=1ndi2},d¯=1n​∑i=1ndi.b_{2,\mathrm{avg}}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{|B_{2}(i)|-1\}=c_{\mathrm{avg}},\qquad\bar{d}\leq b_{2,\mathrm{avg}}\leq\min\left\{n-1,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}^{2}\right\},\qquad\bar{d}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}.

Thus, for independent assignment on an undirected interference graph, the average dependence degree of estimators that use local weights is controlled by the second moment of the degree distribution of the interference graph rather than by the average degree alone. For bounded-degree and sparse Erdős–Renyi interference graphs with bounded expected degree, cavg=O⁡(1)c_{\mathrm{avg}}=O(1). On locally tree-like dd-regular graphs, cavg≍d2c_{\mathrm{avg}}\asymp d^{2}. On a star graph, d¯=O⁡(1)\bar{d}=O(1) but cavg≍nc_{\mathrm{avg}}\asymp n, because all leaves have overlapping closed neighborhoods through the hub. On complete graphs, cavg=n−1c_{\mathrm{avg}}=n-1.

Under dependent randomization designs, two random variables XiX_{i} and XjX_{j} can be dependent even when their closed interference neighborhoods do not overlap. We measure this residual design-induced dependence by the following coefficient.

Definition 19 (Design dependence coefficient).

For two assignment-index sets A,B⊆{1,…,n}A,B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}, define

ρP​(A,B)=sup‖f‖∞≤1,‖g‖∞≤1|CovP⁡{f⁡(𝐙A),g⁡(𝐙B)}|,\rho_{P}(A,B)=\sup_{\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1,\,\|g\|_{\infty}\leq 1}\left|\operatorname{Cov}_{P}\{f(\mathbf{Z}_{A}),g(\mathbf{Z}_{B})\}\right|,

where the supremum is over all measurable functions of the indicated subvectors.

For the local HT/IPW variance bounds below, we use

ρi​j=ρP​(𝒞i,𝒞j),\rho_{ij}=\rho_{P}(\mathcal{C}_{i},\mathcal{C}_{j}),

and

ravg=1n​∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​ρi​j.r_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})\rho_{ij}.

Here ρi​j\rho_{ij} is the pairwise design-dependence coefficient between the two closed-neighborhood assignment subvectors, while ravgr_{\mathrm{avg}} averages only the residual design dependence among pairs whose closed neighborhoods do not overlap. If the design is independent assignment and 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\emptyset, then ρi​j=0\rho_{ij}=0. Complete randomization, cluster randomization, paired designs, and other dependent designs can have ρi​j>0\rho_{ij}>0 even for disjoint closed neighborhoods. These quantities separate overlap of assignment coordinates from dependence induced directly by the randomization design. The variance bounds below therefore separate three sources of variation: the diagonal scale of the HT or importance weights, dependence generated by overlapping closed interference neighborhoods, and residual dependence generated by the randomization design.

4.2 ACE estimation

We first consider nonparametric estimation of an ACE

τACE​(d+,d−)=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(di+)−Yi​(di−)}.\tau_{\mathrm{ACE}}(d^{+},d^{-})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(d_{i}^{+})-Y_{i}(d_{i}^{-})\}.

Write πi(d)=P{Di(𝐙)=d}\pi_{i}(d)=P\{D_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=d\} for the design-induced propensity that unit ii is observed in treatment–exposure combination dd. The generic Horvitz–Thompson estimator is

τ^ACEH​T​(d+,d−)=1n​∑i=1nYio​b​s​{𝟙{Di(𝐙)=di+}πi​(di+)−𝟙{Di(𝐙)=di−}πi​(di−)}.\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}(d^{+},d^{-})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}Y_{i}^{obs}\left\{\frac{\mathds{1}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=d_{i}^{+}\}}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})}-\frac{\mathds{1}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=d_{i}^{-}\}}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})}\right\}.

This is the exposure-mapping Horvitz–Thompson estimator of Aronow and Samii (2017), written here for the generic ACE notation. For the variance bound, let

Hi=1πi​(di+)+1πi​(di−).H_{i}=\frac{1}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})}+\frac{1}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})}.
Proposition 20 (ACE Horvitz–Thompson estimator).

Assume πi​(di+)>0\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})>0 and πi​(di−)>0\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})>0 for all ii. Then τ^ACEH​T​(d+,d−)\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}(d^{+},d^{-}) is design-unbiased for τACE​(d+,d−)\tau_{\mathrm{ACE}}(d^{+},d^{-}) for every potential-outcome table. If, in addition, |Yi​(d)|≤M|Y_{i}(d)|\leq M and the iith summand depends on the assignment only through 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}, then

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T​(d+,d−)}≤M2n2​{∑i=1nHi+∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j​Hi​Hj+∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​ρi​j​Hi​Hj},\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}(d^{+},d^{-})\}\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})\rho_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}\right\},

and if Hi≤HH_{i}\leq H for all ii, then

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T​(d+,d−)}≤M2​{Hn+H2​cavg+ravgn}.\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}(d^{+},d^{-})\}\leq M^{2}\left\{\frac{H}{n}+H^{2}\frac{c_{\mathrm{avg}}+r_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}\right\}.

Consequently, along a sequence of finite populations, the estimator is design-MSE consistent if H+H2​(cavg+ravg)=o⁡(n)H+H^{2}(c_{\mathrm{avg}}+r_{\mathrm{avg}})=o(n).

The proof is given in Appendix D. This proposition separates three sources of variation in the HT estimator: the inverse propensity scores of the relevant potential outcomes Yi​(di+)Y_{i}(d_{i}^{+}) and Yi​(di−)Y_{i}(d_{i}^{-}) (HiH_{i}), the dependence generated by overlapping closed interference neighborhoods (cavgc_{\mathrm{avg}}), and residual dependence from the randomization design (ravgr_{\mathrm{avg}}). The next proposition shows that the inverse-propensity part is not merely an artifact of the HT estimator.

Proposition 21 (Inverse propensity scores for ACEs).

Fix the design PnP_{n} and the induced treatment–exposure combinations Di​(𝐙)D_{i}(\mathbf{Z}). Suppose that τ^n\hat{\tau}_{n} is design-unbiased for τACE​(d+,d−)\tau_{\mathrm{ACE}}(d^{+},d^{-}) for every bounded potential-outcome table. Then

sup|Y|≤MVarPn⁡(τ^n)≥M2n2​maxi​{1πi​(di+)−1,1πi​(di−)−1}.\sup_{|Y|\leq M}\operatorname{Var}_{P_{n}}(\hat{\tau}_{n})\geq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\max_{i}\left\{\frac{1}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})}-1,\,\frac{1}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})}-1\right\}.

The proof is given in Appendix D. This coordinate-wise bound demonstrates that no unbiased estimator of a fixed-exposure ACE can avoid the smallest propensity scores among the relevant treatment–exposure combinations. Below, we show that the diagonal term in the upper bound of Proposition 20 scales identically, and is usually the dominant term when compared to off-diagonal network interference and design dependence terms, giving a matching lower bound for regular graph-unaware designs.

Estimation of DTE and TTE under classical designs.

We now examine when the Horvitz–Thompson estimator can consistently estimate the direct and total treatment effects under standard graph-unaware designs. Proposition 21 provides a matching lower bound: no unbiased estimator can avoid the inverse-propensity scale HH, so the variance conditions we derive are necessary for any design-unbiased estimator, not just the HT. The analysis covers independent designs (Bernoulli, heterogeneous Bernoulli) and exchangeable designs (complete randomization) alike. Proposition 41 (Appendix D.13) shows they share a key property: any specific treatment configuration on aa units has probability exp⁡{−Θ⁡(a)}\exp\{-\Theta(a)\}, so its inverse propensity scales as exp⁡{Θ⁡(a)}\exp\{\Theta(a)\}. Here aa is the number of units the exposure condition constrains — di+1d_{i}+1 for neighborhood-interference targets, nn for arbitrary-interference targets. This exponential-in-aa scaling is the central bottleneck for fixed-exposure ACE estimation and is the only design feature needed below. The variance bound of Proposition 20 formalizes this bottleneck: under independent assignment,

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T}≤M2​{H/n+H2​cavg/n},\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}\}\leq M^{2}\bigl\{H/n+H^{2}c_{\mathrm{avg}}/n\bigr\},

where H=maxi⁡(1/πi​(di+)+1/πi​(di−))H=\max_{i}(1/\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})+1/\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})) and cavgc_{\mathrm{avg}} is the average dependence degree (Lemma 18). We write 𝒱n​(H,c)=H/n+H2​c/n\mathcal{V}_{n}(H,c)=H/n+H^{2}c/n for this scale, suppressing MM. An additional residual dependence term appears under exchangeable designs (Appendix D.3), but it does not change the conclusions.

Tables 1 and 2 summarize HH and the matching lower bound for the DTE and TTE under different representations. The column “HT HH” records the inverse-propensity scale and “LB HH” the matching lower bound. The variance scale column combines HH with the dependence degree b2,avgb_{2,\mathrm{avg}} (which equals cavgc_{\mathrm{avg}} under independent assignment). When HH is exponential, the polynomial dependence is negligible by comparison. For the exposure-mapping rows, let Si=∑j∈NiZjS_{i}=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}Z_{j} denote the number of treated neighbors and Ui=𝟙{Si≥1}U_{i}=\mathds{1}\{S_{i}\geq 1\} the binary any-treated indicator.

Direct treatment effect. The relevant potential outcomes for the DTE are Yi​(1,0Ni)Y_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}}) and Yi​(0,0Ni)Y_{i}(0,0_{N_{i}}) (Definition 15). Under neighborhood interference, the treated arm (1,0Ni)(1,0_{N_{i}}) requires the unit to be treated and all its neighbors to be untreated. Under Bernoulli assignment,

πi​(1,0Ni)=p​(1−p)di,πi​(0,0Ni)=(1−p)di+1,\pi_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}})=p(1-p)^{d_{i}},\qquad\pi_{i}(0,0_{N_{i}})=(1-p)^{d_{i}+1},

so Hi=Θ⁡(eγ​di)H_{i}=\Theta(e^{\gamma d_{i}}) with γ=−log⁡(1−p)\gamma=-\log(1-p) and H=eΘ⁡(dmax)H=e^{\Theta(d_{\max})}. The same exponential scale applies under count, fraction, and binary any-treated exposure mappings for the DTE, since all encode the no-exposure condition as Si=0S_{i}=0 or Ui=0U_{i}=0.

Total treatment effect. The relevant potential outcomes for the TTE are Yi​(1,𝟏Ni)Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{1}_{N_{i}}) and Yi​(0,𝟎Ni)Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}}) (Definition 15). The treated arm requires all neighbors to be treated and the control arm requires all neighbors to be untreated, so HH is exponential in dmaxd_{\max} for every representation in Table 2. Crucially, even the binary any-treated exposure mapping does not remove this scale: the control arm (0,0)(0,0) requires all neighbors to be untreated, with propensity (1−p)di+1(1-p)^{d_{i}+1} decaying exponentially with did_{i}.

Implications for practice. Under classical graph-unaware designs, the relevant potential outcomes for the DTE—Yi​(1,0)Y_{i}(1,0) and Yi​(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0) (Definition 15)—occur with probability exp⁡{−Θ⁡(di)}\exp\{-\Theta(d_{i})\}, leading to an inverse-propensity barrier exponential in the neighborhood degree. For the DTE,

H≍eγ​dmax,γ=−log⁡(1−p),H\asymp e^{\gamma d_{\max}},\qquad\gamma=-\log(1-p),

and the variance bound vanishes only when dmax≲12​γ​log⁡nd_{\max}\lesssim\frac{1}{2\gamma}\log n, i.e., when the degree grows at most logarithmically in nn. This condition is necessary for any unbiased estimator, not just the HT (Proposition 21). For the TTE, the exponential barrier applies across all exposure mappings (Table 2) because both relevant potential outcomes—Yi​(1,𝟏)Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{1}) and Yi​(0,𝟎)Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0})—require every neighbor to be in a specific treatment state.

To overcome this exponential barrier induced by classical designs, we need specialized graph aware designs to estimate ACEs. Section 6 develops such designs: independent-set designs isolate the relevant potential outcomes for the DTE on ego units, while cluster randomized designs increase the probability of the all-treated and all-control conditions needed for the TTE.

4.3 ECE estimation

We now consider estimation of ECEs. Following the definition in Section 3.2, let 𝒬+,𝒬−\mathcal{Q}^{+},\mathcal{Q}^{-} be two allocation policies and Di+​(𝐙),Di−​(𝐙)∈𝒳iD_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z}),D_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})\in\mathcal{X}_{i} the corresponding random treatment–exposure combinations. Define the policy propensities scores as

λi+(d)=𝒬+{Di+(𝐙)=d},λi−(d)=𝒬−{Di−(𝐙)=d},\lambda_{i}^{+}(d)=\mathcal{Q}^{+}\{D_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})=d\},\qquad\lambda_{i}^{-}(d)=\mathcal{Q}^{-}\{D_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})=d\},

so that the ECE can be written as

τECE=1n​∑i=1n∑d∈𝒳iYi​(d)​{λi+​(d)−λi−​(d)}.\tau_{\mathrm{ECE}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{X}_{i}}Y_{i}(d)\{\lambda_{i}^{+}(d)-\lambda_{i}^{-}(d)\}.

Its Horvitz–Thompson estimator has the same form as the ACE estimator of Section 4.2, with the fixed inverse propensity scores of the relevant potential outcomes replaced by importance weights that are ratios of the policy propensity scores to the design propensity scores,

hi+​(𝐳)=λi+​{Di​(𝐳)}πiP​{Di​(𝐳)},hi−​(𝐳)=λi−​{Di​(𝐳)}πiP​{Di​(𝐳)},h_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{z})=\frac{\lambda_{i}^{+}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{z})\}}{\pi_{i}^{P}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{z})\}},\qquad h_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{z})=\frac{\lambda_{i}^{-}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{z})\}}{\pi_{i}^{P}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{z})\}},

with the convention 0/0=00/0=0. Define the diagonal scale

Vi=∑d:πiP​(d)>0{λi+​(d)−λi−​(d)}2πiP​(d),V_{i}=\sum_{d:\pi_{i}^{P}(d)>0}\frac{\{\lambda_{i}^{+}(d)-\lambda_{i}^{-}(d)\}^{2}}{\pi_{i}^{P}(d)},

and the weight bound Hi=sup𝐳{|hi+​(𝐳)|+|hi−​(𝐳)|}H_{i}=\sup_{\mathbf{z}}\{|h_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{z})|+|h_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{z})|\}.

Proposition 22 (ECE importance-weighted estimator).

Suppose λi+​(d)=λi−​(d)=0\lambda_{i}^{+}(d)=\lambda_{i}^{-}(d)=0 whenever πiP​(d)=0\pi_{i}^{P}(d)=0. Then

τ^ECEH​T=1n​∑i=1n{hi+​(𝐙)−hi−​(𝐙)}​Yio​b​s\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ECE}}^{HT}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{h_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})-h_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z})\}Y_{i}^{obs}

is design-unbiased for τECE\tau_{\mathrm{ECE}} for every potential-outcome table. If |Yi​(𝐳)|≤M|Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})|\leq M and the iith summand depends on the assignment only through 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}, then

Var⁡(τ^ECEH​T)≤M2n2​{∑i=1nVi+∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j​Hi​Hj+∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​ρi​j​Hi​Hj}.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ECE}}^{HT})\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}V_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})\rho_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}\right\}.

If Vi≤VV_{i}\leq V and Hi≤HH_{i}\leq H for all ii, then

Var⁡(τ^ECEH​T)≤M2​{Vn+H2​cavg+ravgn},\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ECE}}^{HT})\leq M^{2}\left\{\frac{V}{n}+H^{2}\frac{c_{\mathrm{avg}}+r_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}\right\},

and the estimator is design-MSE consistent if V+H2​(cavg+ravg)=o⁡(n)V+H^{2}(c_{\mathrm{avg}}+r_{\mathrm{avg}})=o(n).

The proof is given in Appendix D. The bound has the same three terms as the ACE bound of Proposition 20: a diagonal term, an interference-dependence term, and a residual design-dependence term. What changes is the diagonal scale. For an ACE, the policy is a point mass at the relevant potential outcomes Yi​(di±)Y_{i}(d_{i}^{\pm}). The importance weights reduce to inverse propensities, and ViV_{i} and HiH_{i} are of the order of 1/πi​(di±)1/\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{\pm}). For an ECE, ViV_{i} and HiH_{i} are governed by the ratios λi±​(d)/πiP​(d)\lambda_{i}^{\pm}(d)/\pi_{i}^{P}(d), and these are large only when the allocation policy places probability on combinations that the design rarely produces. When the allocation policy is the design itself, the ratios are bounded, the diagonal term is O⁡(1/n)O(1/n), and the variance is governed by the dependence terms alone. The next two results make this concrete for the expected direct and indirect effects under Bernoulli policy and design.

Expected direct effect. Under Bernoulli assignment with treatment probabilities pip_{i}, consider the EDE whose policy is the same Bernoulli allocation. The importance weight reduces to the classical Horvitz–Thompson weight

hiEDE​(𝐙)=Zipi−1−Zi1−pi,h_{i}^{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathbf{Z})=\frac{Z_{i}}{p_{i}}-\frac{1-Z_{i}}{1-p_{i}},

so τ^EDEH​T\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT} is the usual difference in weighted means and does not require the interference graph for computation. The weight scales are Vi=Hi=1/pi+1/(1−pi)V_{i}=H_{i}=1/p_{i}+1/(1-p_{i}), which are O⁡(1)O(1) when the treatment probabilities are bounded away from zero and one. No inverse propensity of a rare exposure combination appears in the bound.

Proposition 23 (Variance bound for the EDE estimator).

Let 𝒬p\mathcal{Q}_{p} be a Bernoulli allocation policy, with treatment probabilities bounded away from zero and one. Assume Bernoulli assignment, and sup𝐳|Yi​(𝐳)|≤M\sup_{\mathbf{z}}|Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})|\leq M.
