Then τ^EDEH​T\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT} is design-unbiased for τEDE​(𝒬p)\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q}_{p}), and

VarPn⁡(τ^EDEH​T)≤Cp​M2​1+cavgn,\operatorname{Var}_{P_{n}}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT})\leq C_{p}M^{2}\frac{1+c_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n},

where CpC_{p} depends only on the bounds on the treatment probabilities. In particular, τ^EDEH​T\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT} is design-MSE consistent if cavg=o⁡(n)c_{\mathrm{avg}}=o(n).

The proof is given in Appendix D. This result should be read against the DTE rows of Table 1. The two estimators use the same design and the same interference graph. The DTE estimator must isolate the treatment–exposure combination (1,0Ni)(1,0_{N_{i}}), which the design produces with probability p​(1−p)dip(1-p)^{d_{i}}, so its inverse-propensity scale is H=eΘ⁡(dmax)H=e^{\Theta(d_{\max})} and its full variance scale from Proposition 20 is H/n+H2​cavg/nH/n+H^{2}c_{\mathrm{avg}}/n. The EDE estimator uses every observed outcome, and its variance scale is (1+cavg)/n(1+c_{\mathrm{avg}})/n. On a dd-regular locally tree-like interference graph the comparison is (e2​γ​d​d2)/n(e^{2\gamma d}d^{2})/n against d2/nd^{2}/n: the DTE is consistent only in the logarithmic-degree regime e2​γ​d​d2=o⁡(n)e^{2\gamma d}d^{2}=o(n), i.e., d≲12​γ​log⁡nd\lesssim\frac{1}{2\gamma}\log n, while the EDE HT estimator is consistent whenever d=o⁡(n)d=o(\sqrt{n}). The price of interference for the EDE is not the rarity of any treatment-exposure combination but the dependence among the summands, measured by cavgc_{\mathrm{avg}}.

Expected indirect effect. Graph-aware ECEs that contrast neighbor treatments have larger importance weights. The expected indirect effect sums the weight over neighbors, hiEIE,G​(𝐙)=∑j∈Ni{Zj/pj−(1−Zj)/(1−pj)}h_{i}^{\mathrm{EIE},G}(\mathbf{Z})=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}\{Z_{j}/p_{j}-(1-Z_{j})/(1-p_{j})\}, so Hi≤Cp​diH_{i}\leq C_{p}d_{i} when the treatment probabilities are bounded away from zero and one. The weights grow with the degree, but linearly rather than exponentially.

Corollary 24 (Variance bound for the graph-aware EIE estimator).

Assume the true potential outcomes satisfy neighborhood interference with known neighborhoods NiN_{i}. Assume Bernoulli assignment with treatment probabilities bounded away from zero and one, and assume sup𝐳|Yi​(𝐳)|≤M\sup_{\mathbf{z}}|Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})|\leq M. Then τ^EIEG\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EIE}}^{G} is design-unbiased for τEIE​(π)\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi), and

Var⁡(τ^EIEG)≤Cp​M2n2​{∑idi2+∑i∑j≠ici​j​di​dj},\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EIE}}^{G})\leq\frac{C_{p}M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i}d_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}d_{i}d_{j}\right\},

where di=|Ni|d_{i}=|N_{i}| and ci​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅}c_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\}. If di≤dmaxd_{i}\leq d_{\max} for all ii, then

Var⁡(τ^EIEG)≤Cp​M2​dmax2​1+cavgn.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EIE}}^{G})\leq C_{p}M^{2}d_{\max}^{2}\frac{1+c_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}.

The proof is given in Appendix D. The variance scale dmax2​(1+cavg)/nd_{\max}^{2}(1+c_{\mathrm{avg}})/n is polynomial in the degrees: on a dd-regular locally tree-like graph it is of order d4/nd^{4}/n, so the EIE is consistently estimable whenever d=o⁡(n1/4)d=o(n^{1/4}). As for the EDE, no exponential barrier due to the propensity score appears, and the dependence term dominates the bound.

Appendix D.11 extends the DTE/EDE comparison to arbitrary heterogeneous degree sequences, where it is governed by two graph functionals: exponential moments of the degree sequence for fixed-exposure ACEs, and the average dependence degree for the EDE.

The variance bounds of Section 4 show that classical graph-unaware designs are matched to expected causal effects and pay an exponential cost for average causal effects. Section 5 constructs designs that remove this cost, and Section 6 collects the resulting implications for classical estimators, model-assisted estimation, and the interpretation of positivity under interference.

5 Design-Based Estimation of Average Causal Effects

When classical estimators fail for average causal effects under interference, the failure arises because the realized assignment does not reveal the relevant potential outcomes with sufficient probability. Section 4 shows that under classical graph-unaware designs the target treatment–exposure combinations have inverse propensities that are exponential in the interference degree, and that this cost is unavoidable for any unbiased estimator. One remedy is to modify the experimental design so that those potential outcomes are observed with non-negligible probability. We study designs that control the assignment structure rather than impose an outcome model. The common device is to use the interference graph to create positive correlation within neighborhoods, so that the event that all of a unit’s neighbors are held at a common treatment occurs as a single correlated event rather than as a product of independent events. This replaces the exponential propensity (1−p)di(1-p)^{d_{i}} of a classical design by a propensity that decays only polynomially in the degree did_{i}, and the variance is reduced accordingly. Throughout, we assume that the interference neighborhood is known and that an exposure mapping is specified, and we take the potential outcomes to be uniformly bounded, supi,z,e|Yi​(z,e)|≤M\sup_{i,z,e}|Y_{i}(z,e)|\leq M.

Suppose the target average causal effect has the form

τ=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(di+)−Yi​(di−)},\tau=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(d_{i}^{+})-Y_{i}(d_{i}^{-})\},

where di+d_{i}^{+} and di−d_{i}^{-} are two target treatment–exposure combinations. If the design gives positive probability to both combinations,

πi(di+)=Pr{(Zi,Ei)=di+}>0,πi(di−)=Pr{(Zi,Ei)=di−}>0,\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})=\Pr\{(Z_{i},E_{i})=d_{i}^{+}\}>0,\qquad\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})=\Pr\{(Z_{i},E_{i})=d_{i}^{-}\}>0,

then the treatment–exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator

τ^HTZ​E=1n​∑i=1n{𝟙{(Zi,Ei)=di+}Yiobsπi​(di+)−𝟙{(Zi,Ei)=di−}Yiobsπi​(di−)}\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT}}^{ZE}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{\mathds{1}\{(Z_{i},E_{i})=d_{i}^{+}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})}-\frac{\mathds{1}\{(Z_{i},E_{i})=d_{i}^{-}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})}\right\}

is unbiased for τ\tau. The role of the design is therefore to make the relevant treatment–exposure combinations occur with positive and reasonably large propensity scores.

Proposition 25 (Treatment–exposure HT unbiasedness for ACEs).

Suppose the observed outcome satisfies Yiobs=Yi​(Zi,Ei)Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_{i}(Z_{i},E_{i}). Let

τ=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(di+)−Yi​(di−)},\tau=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(d_{i}^{+})-Y_{i}(d_{i}^{-})\},

and suppose πi​(di+)>0\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})>0 and πi​(di−)>0\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{-})>0 for all ii. Then τ^HTZ​E\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{HT}}^{ZE} is design-unbiased for τ\tau.

The proof is given in Appendix E.

We develop two graph-aware constructions based on independent sets. The first targets the direct treatment effect and uses a distance-one independent set; the second targets the total treatment effect and uses a distance-two independent set. In each case a randomized greedy construction gives focal inclusion probabilities in closed form, and the resulting Horvitz–Thompson estimator has mean squared error that is polynomial, rather than exponential, in the interference degree. We then discuss cluster randomized designs, whose polynomial behavior is conditional on the clustering being aligned with the graph.

5.1 Independent set designs for the direct treatment effect

The direct treatment effect

τD=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1,𝟎Ni)−Yi​(0,𝟎Ni)}\tau^{D}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})-Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})\}

contrasts the treated and control potential outcomes of a unit whose neighbors are all held at control. Both arms require the no-exposure condition ZNi=𝟎Z_{N_{i}}=\mathbf{0}; they differ only in the unit’s own treatment. Consequently two units ii and jj that share a neighbor k∈Ni∩Njk\in N_{i}\cap N_{j} impose the same requirement Zk=0Z_{k}=0, so there is no conflict between their target conditions. A distance-one independent set, in which selected units are mutually non-adjacent but may share neighbors, therefore suffices.

We construct a random independent set of ego units by a randomized greedy rule, and randomize treatment among the egos while holding their neighbors at control. Units outside the independent set act as alter units that buffer the egos from interference.

Design (IS-1).

  1. (1)

    Draw U1,…,UnU_{1},\dots,U_{n} independently from the uniform distribution on [0,1][0,1].

  2. (2)

    Let ℐ={i:Ui<Uk​ for all ​k∈Ni}\mathcal{I}=\{i:U_{i}<U_{k}\text{ for all }k\in N_{i}\} be the set of units whose draw is the strict minimum in their closed neighborhood {i}∪Ni\{i\}\cup N_{i}. The set ℐ\mathcal{I} is an independent set almost surely.

  3. (3)

    For each ego i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, draw Bi∼Bernoulli⁡(q)B_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q) independently, set Zi=BiZ_{i}=B_{i}, and set Zk=0Z_{k}=0 for all k∈Nik\in N_{i}.

  4. (4)

    Assign any unit not fixed by step (3) a treatment by a prespecified rule that does not overwrite the constraints of step (3).

The construction is graph-aware: whether ii is an ego depends only on the draws in its closed neighborhood. If two egos ii and jj share a neighbor kk, step (3) sets Zk=0Z_{k}=0 from both, so the assignment is consistent regardless of how many egos claim kk. Because the event {i∈ℐ}\{i\in\mathcal{I}\} is determined within {i}∪Ni\{i\}\cup N_{i}, the inclusion probability is available in closed form.

Lemma 26 (Inclusion and reveal probabilities under IS-1).

Under the design IS-1,

Pr⁡(i∈ℐ)=1di+1.\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I})=\frac{1}{d_{i}+1}.

Let Fi(1)={i∈ℐ,Bi=1}F_{i}^{(1)}=\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ B_{i}=1\} and Fi(0)={i∈ℐ,Bi=0}F_{i}^{(0)}=\{i\in\mathcal{I},\ B_{i}=0\} be the focal reveal events. On Fi(1)F_{i}^{(1)} the assignment satisfies (Zi,ZNi)=(1,𝟎)(Z_{i},Z_{N_{i}})=(1,\mathbf{0}), and on Fi(0)F_{i}^{(0)} it satisfies (Zi,ZNi)=(0,𝟎)(Z_{i},Z_{N_{i}})=(0,\mathbf{0}), so

ρi(1):=Pr⁡(Fi(1))=qdi+1,ρi(0):=Pr⁡(Fi(0))=1−qdi+1.\rho_{i}^{(1)}:=\Pr(F_{i}^{(1)})=\frac{q}{d_{i}+1},\qquad\rho_{i}^{(0)}:=\Pr(F_{i}^{(0)})=\frac{1-q}{d_{i}+1}.

The proof is given in Appendix E. The inclusion probability follows from the symmetry of the di+1d_{i}+1 independent draws in the closed neighborhood, and the reveal probabilities follow from the independent treatment coin BiB_{i}. The focal reveal probabilities are exact and do not require simulation. They are stated for the focal events rather than for the raw exposure events {Zi=s,ZNi=𝟎}\{Z_{i}=s,Z_{N_{i}}=\mathbf{0}\}, because non-ego units may also happen to satisfy the no-exposure condition depending on the leftover rule in step (4); the estimator below uses only the focal events, whose probabilities are known exactly. Taking q=12q=\tfrac{1}{2} gives the symmetric values ρi(1)=ρi(0)=1/{2​(di+1)}\rho_{i}^{(1)}=\rho_{i}^{(0)}=1/\{2(d_{i}+1)\}.

The focal Horvitz–Thompson estimator for the direct treatment effect is

τ^ISD=1n​∑i=1n{𝟙​{Fi(1)}​Yiobsρi(1)−𝟙​{Fi(0)}​Yiobsρi(0)},\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{\mathds{1}\{F_{i}^{(1)}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\rho_{i}^{(1)}}-\frac{\mathds{1}\{F_{i}^{(0)}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\rho_{i}^{(0)}}\right\},

which at q=12q=\tfrac{1}{2} reduces to

τ^ISD=2n​∑i=1n(di+1)​{𝟙​{Fi(1)}​Yiobs−𝟙​{Fi(0)}​Yiobs}.\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(d_{i}+1)\left\{\mathds{1}\{F_{i}^{(1)}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\mathds{1}\{F_{i}^{(0)}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right\}.
Proposition 27 (Unbiasedness of the IS-1 estimator).

Under the design IS-1 with q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1), the estimator τ^ISD\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D} is design-unbiased for the direct treatment effect, 𝔼⁡[τ^ISD]=τD\mathbb{E}[\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D}]=\tau^{D}.

The proof is the same Horvitz–Thompson calculation as Proposition 25, applied to the focal reveal events rather than to the raw treatment–exposure events. On Fi(1)F_{i}^{(1)} and Fi(0)F_{i}^{(0)} the observed outcome equals the corresponding direct-effect potential outcome, and the focal probabilities ρi(1),ρi(0)\rho_{i}^{(1)},\rho_{i}^{(0)} are positive and known.

The variance of the estimator is controlled by the closed-neighborhood inclusion probabilities and by the dependence among egos that lie within distance two of one another. Write δi=Yi​(1,𝟎Ni)−Yi​(0,𝟎Ni)\delta_{i}=Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})-Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}}) and pi=Pr⁡(i∈ℐ)=1/(di+1)p_{i}=\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I})=1/(d_{i}+1).

Proposition 28 (Variance of the IS-1 estimator).

Under the design IS-1 with q=12q=\tfrac{1}{2}, the estimator satisfies the exact identity

n2Var(τ^ISD)=∑i=1nVar(Wi)+∑i≠j:distG​(i,j)≤2δiδj(Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ)pi​pj−1),n^{2}\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(W_{i})+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j:\ \mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\leq 2\end{subarray}}\delta_{i}\delta_{j}\left(\frac{\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I})}{p_{i}p_{j}}-1\right),

where Wi=2(di+1)𝟙{i∈ℐ}{Yi(1,𝟎Ni)Bi−Yi(0,𝟎Ni)(1−Bi)}W_{i}=2(d_{i}+1)\mathds{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}\}\{Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})B_{i}-Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})(1-B_{i})\}. For non-adjacent i,ji,j sharing si​j=|Ni∩Nj|s_{ij}=|N_{i}\cap N_{j}| common neighbors, Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ)/(pi​pj)=(di+dj+2)/(di+dj+2−si​j)\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I})/(p_{i}p_{j})=(d_{i}+d_{j}+2)/(d_{i}+d_{j}+2-s_{ij}), while Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ)=0\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I})=0 when ii and jj are adjacent. Consequently, uniformly over |Yi​(⋅)|≤M|Y_{i}(\cdot)|\leq M,

Var(τ^ISD)≤4​M2n2∑i=1n(di+1)+4​M2n2[2|E|+∑i≠j:i≁j,si​j≥1si​jdi+dj+2−si​j].\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D})\leq\frac{4M^{2}}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(d_{i}+1)+\frac{4M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left[2|E|+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j:\ i\not\sim j,\ s_{ij}\geq 1\end{subarray}}\frac{s_{ij}}{d_{i}+d_{j}+2-s_{ij}}\right].

The proof is given in Appendix E. The first term is a diagonal contribution of order n−2​∑i(di+1)n^{-2}\sum_{i}(d_{i}+1); the second collects the dependence among egos whose closed neighborhoods overlap, that is, egos within graph distance two.

Corollary 29 (Polynomial rate for the direct treatment effect).

If GG is dd-regular and locally tree-like, in the sense that every pair of non-adjacent vertices has at most a bounded number of common neighbors (si​j=O⁡(1)s_{ij}=O(1)), then

Var⁡(τ^ISD)=O⁡(M2​dn).\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D})=O\!\left(\frac{M^{2}d}{n}\right).

For a general dd-regular graph, the second-moment bound gives the cruder rate

Var⁡(τ^ISD)=O⁡(M2​d2n),\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D})=O\!\left(\frac{M^{2}d^{2}}{n}\right),

since on any dd-regular graph the crude bound evaluates to 4​M2​(n+n​d+n​d2)/n24M^{2}(n+nd+nd^{2})/n^{2}. For an arbitrary graph, the crude second-moment bound gives

Var⁡(τ^ISD)≤4​M2n2​[n+∑idi+∑idi2]=O⁡(M2​(1+d¯+d2¯)n),d2¯=1n​∑idi2.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{D})\leq\frac{4M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left[n+\sum_{i}d_{i}+\sum_{i}d_{i}^{2}\right]=O\!\left(\frac{M^{2}\,(1+\bar{d}+\overline{d^{2}})}{n}\right),\qquad\overline{d^{2}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}d_{i}^{2}.

The proof is given in Appendix E. Under a Bernoulli design the same estimand requires the no-exposure condition, whose propensity p​(1−p)dip(1-p)^{d_{i}} is exponentially small in did_{i}, and the resulting variance is exponential in the average degree by Proposition 21. The IS-1 design replaces this exponential cost by dependence that is polynomial in the degree sequence. The bound of Corollary 29 holds for arbitrary, not necessarily regular, interference graphs: it is of order M2​(1+d¯+d2¯)/nM^{2}(1+\bar{d}+\overline{d^{2}})/n, so this estimator is consistent whenever d2¯=o⁡(n)\overline{d^{2}}=o(n). This is the same second-moment condition on the degree sequence under which the expected direct effect is consistent by the generic dependence-graph bound. On dd-regular graphs that are locally tree-like, in the sense that non-adjacent vertices share at most a bounded number of common neighbors, the sharper rate O⁡(M2​d¯/n)O(M^{2}\bar{d}/n) holds. On a general dd-regular graph the wedge sum ∑i≠j:i≁jsi​j/(di+dj+2−si​j)\sum_{i\neq j:\ i\not\sim j}s_{ij}/(d_{i}+d_{j}+2-s_{ij}) can be as large as Θ⁡(n​d2)\Theta(nd^{2}) when closed neighborhoods overlap heavily, so the crude rate O⁡(M2​d2/n)O(M^{2}d^{2}/n) is the best that the second-moment bound certifies in general. Figure 3 illustrates the effect: on a fixed family of graphs, the error of the independent set estimator remains nearly flat in the degree, whereas under a Bernoulli design it grows exponentially. For irregular graphs with high-degree hubs the crude bound can be larger, and a hub-aware modification of the focal sampling may control it, though we do not pursue this refinement here. For extreme hub graphs such as a star, this particular randomized local-minimum IS-1 design has a non-vanishing second-moment bound; this indicates a limitation of the simple construction rather than a universal impossibility theorem.

5.2 Independent set designs for the total treatment effect

The total treatment effect

τT=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1,ei𝟏)−Yi​(0,0)},ei𝟏=fi​(𝟏Ni),\tau^{T}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})-Y_{i}(0,0)\},\qquad e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}=f_{i}(\mathbf{1}_{N_{i}}),

contrasts the all-treated and all-control regimes on the closed neighborhood {i}∪Ni\{i\}\cup N_{i}. Unlike the direct treatment effect, the two arms now impose opposite requirements on a shared neighbor: if egos ii and jj share a neighbor kk and ii is on the treated side while jj is on the control side, then ii requires Zk=1Z_{k}=1 and jj requires Zk=0Z_{k}=0, a direct conflict. Avoiding such conflicts requires that egos have disjoint closed neighborhoods, that is, that they be at graph distance at least three. This is a distance-two independent set, obtained by running the randomized greedy rule on the radius-two balls.

For a unit ii let Bi(2)={k:distG​(i,k)≤2}B_{i}^{(2)}=\{k:\mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,k)\leq 2\} denote its radius-two ball and bi=|Bi(2)|b_{i}=|B_{i}^{(2)}| its size. Since the neighborhood is contained in the ball,

di+1≤bi≤1+di+∑j∈Ni(dj−1)≤1+di​dmax.d_{i}+1\leq b_{i}\leq 1+d_{i}+\sum_{j\in N_{i}}(d_{j}-1)\leq 1+d_{i}d_{\max}.

On dd-regular locally tree-like graphs this gives bi=1+d+d⁡(d−1)=d2+1b_{i}=1+d+d(d-1)=d^{2}+1.

Design (IS-2).

  1. (1)

    Draw U1,…,UnU_{1},\dots,U_{n} independently from the uniform distribution on [0,1][0,1].

  2. (2)

    Let ℐ2={i:Ui<Uk​ for all ​k∈Bi(2)∖{i}}\mathcal{I}_{2}=\{i:U_{i}<U_{k}\text{ for all }k\in B_{i}^{(2)}\setminus\{i\}\} be the set of units whose draw is the strict minimum in their radius-two ball. The set ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} is a distance-two independent set almost surely.

  3. (3)

    For each ego i∈ℐ2i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}, draw Ri∼Bernoulli⁡(12)R_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\tfrac{1}{2}) independently, and set Zk=RiZ_{k}=R_{i} for all k∈{i}∪Nik\in\{i\}\cup N_{i}.

  4. (4)

    Assign any unit not fixed by step (3) an independent Bernoulli⁡(12)\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\tfrac{1}{2}) treatment.

Because egos are at distance at least three, their closed neighborhoods are disjoint and step (3) is free of conflicts. Since the outcome of an ego depends only on the assignment of its closed neighborhood, which is entirely fixed in step (3), the leftover assignments in step (4) do not affect the revealed outcomes of egos.

Lemma 30 (Inclusion and reveal probabilities under IS-2).

Under the design IS-2,

Pr⁡(i∈ℐ2)=1bi,ρi(1):=Pr⁡(i∈ℐ2,Ri=1)=12​bi,ρi(0):=Pr⁡(i∈ℐ2,Ri=0)=12​bi.\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I}_{2})=\frac{1}{b_{i}},\qquad\rho_{i}^{(1)}:=\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=1)=\frac{1}{2b_{i}},\qquad\rho_{i}^{(0)}:=\Pr(i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=0)=\frac{1}{2b_{i}}.

On these focal events the assignment reveals the corresponding all-treated or all-control potential outcome. In particular, if the radius-two balls are polynomially bounded in the interference degree scale, the inverse focal probabilities are polynomial as well.

The proof is given in Appendix E. The focal Horvitz–Thompson estimator for the total treatment effect is

τ^IST=2n∑i∈ℐ2bi{𝟙{Ri=1}Yiobs−𝟙{Ri=0}Yiobs}.\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T}=\frac{2}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}}b_{i}\left\{\mathds{1}\{R_{i}=1\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}-\mathds{1}\{R_{i}=0\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right\}.
Proposition 31 (Unbiasedness and variance of the IS-2 estimator).

Under the design IS-2, the estimator τ^IST\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T} is design-unbiased for the total treatment effect. The unbiasedness is with respect to the focal reveal events (i∈ℐ2,Ri=1)(i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=1) and (i∈ℐ2,Ri=0)(i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=0), each of which implies the corresponding treatment–exposure condition. Writing Δi=Yi​(1,ei𝟏)−Yi​(0,0)\Delta_{i}=Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})-Y_{i}(0,0) and qi=1/biq_{i}=1/b_{i}, it satisfies the exact identity

n2Var(τ^IST)=∑i=1nVar(Vi)+∑i≠j:Bi(2)∩Bj(2)≠∅ΔiΔj(Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ2)qi​qj−1),n^{2}\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(V_{i})+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j:\ B_{i}^{(2)}\cap B_{j}^{(2)}\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j}\left(\frac{\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I}_{2})}{q_{i}q_{j}}-1\right),

where Vi=2bi𝟙{i∈ℐ2}{Yi(1,ei𝟏)Ri−Yi(0,0)(1−Ri)}V_{i}=2b_{i}\mathds{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}\}\{Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})R_{i}-Y_{i}(0,0)(1-R_{i})\}. If distG​(i,j)≤2\mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\leq 2, then Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ2)=0\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I}_{2})=0; if distG​(i,j)∈{3,4}\mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\in\{3,4\} and s=|Bi(2)∩Bj(2)|≥1s=|B_{i}^{(2)}\cap B_{j}^{(2)}|\geq 1, then the ratio equals (bi+bj)/(bi+bj−s)(b_{i}+b_{j})/(b_{i}+b_{j}-s). Consequently, uniformly over |Yi​(⋅)|≤M|Y_{i}(\cdot)|\leq M,

Var(τ^IST)≤4​M2n2∑i=1nbi+4​M2n2∑i≠j:distG​(i,j)≤21+4​M2n2∑i≠j:distG​(i,j)∈{3,4},si​j(2)≥1si​j(2)bi+bj−si​j(2),si​j(2)=|Bi(2)∩Bj(2)|.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T})\leq\frac{4M^{2}}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}b_{i}+\frac{4M^{2}}{n^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j:\ \mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\leq 2\end{subarray}}1+\frac{4M^{2}}{n^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j:\ \mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\in\{3,4\},\ s_{ij}^{(2)}\geq 1\end{subarray}}\frac{s_{ij}^{(2)}}{b_{i}+b_{j}-s_{ij}^{(2)}},\qquad s_{ij}^{(2)}=|B_{i}^{(2)}\cap B_{j}^{(2)}|.

The proof is given in Appendix E.

Corollary 32 (Polynomial rate for the total treatment effect).

On dd-regular graphs that are locally tree-like, the diagonal and distance-two exclusion terms are of order M2​d2/nM^{2}d^{2}/n, and the positive radius-two overlap term contributes at most the same order (distance-three partners contribute M2​d/nM^{2}d/n and distance-four partners M2​d2/nM^{2}d^{2}/n), so

Var⁡(τ^IST)=O⁡(M2​d2n).\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T})=O\!\left(\frac{M^{2}d^{2}}{n}\right).

For an arbitrary graph, the universal bound is Var⁡(τ^IST)=O⁡(M2​b2¯/n)\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T})=O(M^{2}\overline{b^{2}}/n) with b2¯=n−1​∑ibi2\overline{b^{2}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}b_{i}^{2}.

Since di≤dmaxd_{i}\leq d_{\max} and bi≤1+di​dmaxb_{i}\leq 1+d_{i}d_{\max}, the bounds in Corollaries 29 and 32 give variance bounds of order O⁡(M2​(1+dmax2)/n)O(M^{2}(1+d_{\max}^{2})/n) for IS-1 and O⁡(M2​(1+dmax4)/n)O(M^{2}(1+d_{\max}^{4})/n) for IS-2 on every interference graph. The proof is given in Appendix E. Under a Bernoulli design the total treatment effect requires the all-treated condition on the closed neighborhood, whose propensity pdi+1p^{d_{i}+1} is again exponentially small in did_{i}. On locally tree-like dd-regular graphs, the IS-2 design attains the polynomial rate O⁡(M2​d2/n)O(M^{2}d^{2}/n), the same degree order as the expected direct effect under a Bernoulli design established in Proposition 23. On arbitrary graphs the rate is governed by the radius-two ball sizes bib_{i}. The exponential separation between average and expected causal effects under classical designs is therefore not intrinsic to the estimands: with a design aligned to the estimand, the total treatment effect can be estimated at polynomial rates. The direct treatment effect is easier still, since Corollary 29 gives the smaller rate O⁡(M2​d¯/n)O(M^{2}\bar{d}/n) on locally tree-like regular graphs.

5.3 Independent set designs for indirect effects

Indirect (spillover) effects ask how the outcome of a unit is affected by the treatment of others, its own treatment held fixed. A recurring target in network experiments is the effect of treating a selected set of influencers on an average unit: seeding experiments assign treatment to a sparse set of influential units and measure the response of otherwise untreated peers exposed to a treated influencer (Paluck et al., 2016; Aral and Walker, 2012; Aral et al., 2013; Bond et al., 2012). Under the any-treated exposure map (3.6), which records Ui=1U_{i}=1 whenever at least one neighbor of ii is treated, this target is the two-level average indirect effect τIE​(z,0,1)=n−1​∑i{Yi​(z,1)−Yi​(z,0)}\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(z;0,1)=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\{Y_{i}(z,1)-Y_{i}(z,0)\} of Section 3.1: a comparison of the no-exposure level ea=0e_{a}=0 and the any-treated level eb=1e_{b}=1 with the unit’s own treatment zz fixed (z=0z=0 for an untreated peer). Estimators of spillover effects under two-stage and independent-set randomization are developed in Baird et al. (2018); Basse and Feller (2018); Cai et al. (2024), and two-level exposure contrasts of this form are the fixed-exposure analogue of the allocation-averaged estimand class studied by Viviano (2026). The uncompressed special cases contrast the fully exposed and unexposed neighborhood regimes, with the unit’s own treatment held fixed:

τIEC=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(0,ei𝟏)−Yi​(0,0)},τIET=1n​∑i=1n{Yi​(1,ei𝟏)−Yi​(1,0)}.\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(0,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})-Y_{i}(0,0)\},\qquad\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\{Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})-Y_{i}(1,0)\}.

Both arms of an indirect contrast fix an extreme neighborhood regime, and the exponential barrier of Section 4 applies exactly as it does to the direct and total effects. Under a Bernoulli design with probability pp, the unexposed arm has propensity Pr⁡(Zi=z†)​(1−p)di\Pr(Z_{i}=z^{\dagger})(1-p)^{d_{i}}, the any-treated arm has propensity Pr⁡(Zi=z†)​(1−(1−p)di)\Pr(Z_{i}=z^{\dagger})(1-(1-p)^{d_{i}}), and the full-exposure arm has propensity Pr⁡(Zi=z†)​pdi\Pr(Z_{i}=z^{\dagger})\,p^{d_{i}}, where z†z^{\dagger} is the own-treatment level of the estimand and all but the any-treated propensity are exponentially small in the degree. Every indirect effect that fixes a rare exposure regime is therefore exponentially costly under a graph-unaware design.

The distance-two independent set construction of Section 5.2 removes this barrier for the indirect effects with a single modification. On the ego set ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2}, hold each ego’s own treatment at the level z†z^{\dagger} required by the estimand (z†=0z^{\dagger}=0 for τIEC\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}} and for control units; z†=1z^{\dagger}=1 for τIET\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}), and assign the ego’s neighborhood the common value Ri∈{0,1}R_{i}\in\{0,1\} by an independent fair coin. An ego then reveals (z†,ei𝟏)(z^{\dagger},e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}) when Ri=1R_{i}=1 and (z†,0)(z^{\dagger},0) when Ri=0R_{i}=0, each with focal probability 1/(2​bi)1/(2b_{i}).

Proposition 33 (Independent set designs for indirect effects).

Under the modified distance-two independent set design above, the focal Horvitz–Thompson estimator is design-unbiased, with focal reveal probabilities 1/(2​bi)1/(2b_{i}) for both arms, for the any-treated indirect effects τIE​(0,0,1)\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(0;0,1) and τIE​(1,0,1)\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(1;0,1) under the exposure map (3.6), and for the full-exposure versions τIEC\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}} (z†=0z^{\dagger}=0) and τIET\tau_{\mathrm{IET}} (z†=1z^{\dagger}=1). Its variance satisfies the bound of Proposition 31, and on locally tree-like dd-regular graphs

Var⁡(τ^IS)=O⁡(M2​d2¯n),\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}})=O\!\left(\frac{M^{2}\overline{d^{2}}}{n}\right),

matching the rate of the total treatment effect and of the expected direct effect on this graph class.

The proof is identical to that of Proposition 31: fixing the ego’s own treatment changes neither the inclusion probabilities nor the covariance structure, and only the pair of revealed treatment–exposure arms differs. No modification of the design is needed for the coarsened two-level estimand. Because the all-treated arm realizes the any-treated level Ui=1U_{i}=1 and the all-control arm realizes Ui=0U_{i}=0 under (3.6), the polarized design estimates τIE​(z†,0,1)\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(z^{\dagger};0,1) with the same focal probabilities 1/(2​bi)1/(2b_{i}). More generally, any monotone exposure map that takes the value 11 on the all-treated vector and 00 on the all-control vector yields the same two realized levels, so the same estimator applies to the corresponding coarsened two-level indirect effect. The coarsening is therefore free for the polarized design: it changes only the exposure interpretation, not the assignment, and it can only shorten the distance between the two levels of the contrast.

Sparse seeding with the distance-one independent set.

Influencer-seeding experiments treat a sparse, well-separated set of units and measure the responses of their nontreated alters. The distance-one independent set ℐ\mathcal{I} of Section 5.1 is exactly such a set: egos are mutually non-adjacent, and on typical graphs each alter is adjacent to a controlled number of egos. Treating each ego with an independent coin Bi∼Bernoulli⁡(q)B_{i}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(q) and setting all non-ego units to control yields the sparse seeding design: the treated influencers are the egos with Bi=1B_{i}=1, and an alter’s any-treated indicator (3.6) equals 11 precisely when at least one of its neighbors is a treated ego. Let Ki=|ℐ∩Ni|K_{i}=|\mathcal{I}\cap N_{i}| be the number of ego neighbors of unit ii. Because II is an independent set, an ego has no ego neighbors; the unit ii consequently reveals (0,1)(0,1) on the event

Fi(1)={∑j∈NiBj𝟙{j∈ℐ}≥1}i.e.{Zi=0,Ui=1},F_{i}^{(1)}=\Big\{\textstyle\sum_{j\in N_{i}}B_{j}\mathds{1}\{j\in\mathcal{I}\}\geq 1\Big\}\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\{Z_{i}=0,\ U_{i}=1\},

and reveals (0,0)(0,0) on Fi(0)={Zi=0}∖Fi(1)F_{i}^{(0)}=\{Z_{i}=0\}\setminus F_{i}^{(1)}, with Fi(1)∪Fi(0)={Zi=0}F_{i}^{(1)}\cup F_{i}^{(0)}=\{Z_{i}=0\}. The focal probabilities are

ρi(1)=𝔼⁡[1−(1−q)Ki],ρi(0)=𝔼⁡[(1−q)Ki]−qdi+1.\rho_{i}^{(1)}=\mathbb{E}\big[1-(1-q)^{K_{i}}\big],\qquad\rho_{i}^{(0)}=\mathbb{E}\big[(1-q)^{K_{i}}\big]-\frac{q}{d_{i}+1}. (5.1)

Both are positive for every unit with degree at least one.

Proposition 34 (Sparse seeding estimates the influencer spillover effect).

Under the sparse seeding design with q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) and no isolated units, the focal Horvitz–Thompson estimator

τ^seed=1n​∑i=1n{𝟙​{Fi(1)}​Yiobsρi(1)−𝟙​{Fi(0)}​Yiobsρi(0)}\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{seed}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Big\{\frac{\mathds{1}\{F_{i}^{(1)}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\rho_{i}^{(1)}}-\frac{\mathds{1}\{F_{i}^{(0)}\}Y_{i}^{\mathrm{obs}}}{\rho_{i}^{(0)}}\Big\}

is design-unbiased for the influencer spillover effect τIE​(0,0,1)\tau_{\mathrm{IE}}(0;0,1) under the any-treated exposure map (3.6). On a locally tree-like dd-regular graph, Ki⇒Poisson⁡(1)K_{i}\Rightarrow\mathrm{Poisson}(1) and, as d→∞d\to\infty,

ρi(1)→1−e−q,ρi(0)→e−q:\rho_{i}^{(1)}\to 1-e^{-q},\qquad\rho_{i}^{(0)}\to e^{-q}:

both arms have constant focal probability, independent of nn and of the degree, and the inverse-propensity weights 1/ρi(1)+1/ρi(0)1/\rho_{i}^{(1)}+1/\rho_{i}^{(0)} are O⁡(1)O(1). The covariance structure is inherited from the ego draws and has the radius-two range of Proposition 28, so the variance satisfies the generic bound of Proposition 20; on locally tree-like dd-regular graphs the diagonal term is O⁡(M2/n)O(M^{2}/n), removing the inverse-propensity barrier entirely for this estimand.

The proof is given in Appendix E. The constant-order focal probabilities contrast sharply with the focal probability 1/(2​bi)=O⁡(1/d2)1/(2b_{i})=O(1/d^{2}) of the full-exposure design of Proposition 33: the coarsening to the any-treated level eb=1e_{b}=1 is what converts the exponentially rare all-treated event into a condition–“at least one treated neighbor”–that has constant probability under sparse seeding. The hub caveat is that the guarantee is tied to the ego-neighborhood count KiK_{i} being O⁡(1)O(1) in expectation. On a star, for example, the center faces up to dd simultaneously eligible ego candidates among its leaves and ρc(0)=∫01(1−q​u)d​𝑑u=O⁡(1/(q​d))\rho_{c}^{(0)}=\int_{0}^{1}(1-qu)^{d}\,du=O(1/(qd)): the unexposed arm of the hub decays polynomially rather than staying constant, so the invertible focal weights grow linearly in the hub degree. The constant-propensity claim is therefore restricted to graph families in which ego-neighborhoods are small in expectation, such as locally tree-like dd-regular graphs and, more generally, graphs of bounded degree. Thus the distance-one construction of Section 5.1, run as a seeding experiment, estimates the influencer spillover effect at constant focal propensities on exactly the bounded-degree families where the intervention is well-defined. In every case the exponential separation between average and expected causal effects under classical designs is a consequence of graph-unaware assignment, not a property of the estimand.

5.4 Cluster randomized designs

A cluster randomized design partitions the units into disjoint clusters 𝒞={C1,…,CK}\mathcal{C}=\{C_{1},\dots,C_{K}\} and assigns a common treatment to all units in a cluster, drawing the cluster-level indicators W1,…,WKW_{1},\dots,W_{K} according to a specified scheme. A unit ii reveals Yi​(1,ei𝟏)Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}) when its cluster and all clusters meeting its neighborhood are treated, and reveals Yi​(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0) when they are all controlled. Provided the induced propensities πi​(1,ei𝟏)\pi_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}) and πi​(0,0)\pi_{i}(0,0) are positive, the treatment–exposure Horvitz–Thompson estimator of Proposition 25 is unbiased for the total treatment effect; explicit expressions for these propensities under graph cluster randomization are given by Ugander et al. (2013).

The polynomial behavior of cluster randomization is, however, conditional on the clustering being aligned with the graph. Let mim_{i} denote the number of distinct clusters met by the closed neighborhood {i}∪Ni\{i\}\cup N_{i}. Under independent cluster-level assignment with probability 12\tfrac{1}{2}, the all-treated condition requires all mim_{i} of these clusters to be treated, so

πi​(1,ei𝟏)=(12)mi,\pi_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})=\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\Big)^{m_{i}},

and the inverse propensity is 2mi2^{m_{i}}, exponential in the number of clusters the neighborhood spans rather than in the degree. When the clustering places each closed neighborhood inside a bounded number of clusters, mi=O⁡(1)m_{i}=O(1) and the propensity is bounded below by a constant. Low-boundary or low-conductance partitions can have this property in clustered graphs, but the relevant design quantity is the neighborhood cluster count mim_{i} itself. On graphs for which every practical balanced clustering splits many neighborhoods across a growing number of clusters, mim_{i} grows with the degree, and the exponential cost reappears. Cluster randomization therefore trades an exponential dependence on degree for an exponential dependence on the neighborhood boundary, and removes the estimation barrier only when the chosen clustering is aligned with the interference graph. The independent set design IS-2 gives a graph-agnostic polynomial upper bound for the total treatment effect, while cluster designs can be sharper on graphs with strong community structure.

6 Implications for Designs, Estimators, and Models

The variance bounds of Section 4 have several implications for the design and analysis of experiments under interference. We collect them here.

6.1 Classical designs and estimators target expected causal effects

Bernoulli and completely randomized designs, analyzed with the difference-in-means estimator, are the tools most commonly used in practice. That these classical tools estimate an expected causal effect rather than an average causal effect under interference is well known (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008; Sävje et al., 2017): the difference-in-means estimator targets the expected direct effect, obtained by averaging the unit-level direct effect over the exposure induced by the design. Under a Bernoulli design, the difference-in-means estimator is design-unbiased for the expected direct effect; by Proposition 23, its variance is of order (1+cavg)/n(1+c_{\mathrm{avg}})/n, and its computation does not require the knowledge of interference graph. However, the expected direct effect is policy dependent, and it mixes direct treatment effect and interference effects, as shown in Proposition 12 which uses the non-parametric linear decomposition.

The same design and estimator are ill-suited to non-parametrically estimate average causal effects. The direct treatment effect is a contrast of the potential outcomes Yi​(1,𝟎Ni)Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}}) and Yi​(0,𝟎Ni)Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}}), and under a Bernoulli design the cell (1,𝟎Ni)(1,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}}) is observed with probability p​(1−p)dip(1-p)^{d_{i}}. By Proposition 21, the variance of any graph unaware design-unbiased estimator of the direct treatment effect is then exponential in the interference degree, a similar result holds for the total treatment effect. Moreover, the difference-in-means estimator is not consistent for the direct treatment effect: its probability limit is the expected direct effect, so it carries a bias equal to the expected treatment–exposure interaction C¯\overline{C}, which is zero only under additivity. Classical estimators are therefore appropriate for expected causal effects such as the expected direct effect, but not for average causal effects such as the direct and total treatment effects.

6.2 Positivity and overlap for average causal effects

Changing the exposure mapping does not provide an escape. As shown in Section 4, the direct treatment effect requires the no-exposure potential outcome under any mapping, so its propensity remains exponentially small in the degree. The difficulty is a failure of positivity for the relevant treatment–exposure combination, the analogue under interference of the overlap condition in observational studies. On interference graphs with high-degree units this failure is severe, and a fixed-exposure average causal effect can be identified only on the subpopulation of units whose neighborhoods are small enough to provide adequate overlap.

6.3 Model-assisted estimation of average causal effects

A second strategy is available when one is willing to impose outcome model restrictions on the potential outcomes. The non-parametric decomposition Yi​(z,e)=Ai​(z)+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e)Y_{i}(z,e)=A_{i}(z)+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e) suggests a natural class of working models: a restriction on the spillover and interaction components BiB_{i} and CiC_{i} relates the nuisance potential outcomes to the relevant ones, so that units that reveal nuisance potential outcomes also become informative for the estimand. The simplest such restriction is additivity, Ci≡0C_{i}\equiv 0, under which the difference-in-means estimator is consistent for the direct treatment effect, since the bias C¯\overline{C} then vanishes. More generally, a working model can be used within a model-assisted estimator, such as a generalized regression estimator, that retains a design-based target while borrowing information across treatment–exposure cells. Such estimators trade the exponential cost of the inverse propensity for sensitivity to misspecification of the working model. Model-assisted estimators of this kind under interference are developed in Karwa and Airoldi (2018).

7 Numerical illustration

We illustrate the estimation gap between ACEs and ECEs on simulated experiments. The interference graph, the exposure mapping, and the potential outcomes are fixed in advance, and the only source of randomness is the treatment assignment.

We draw the interference graph from two random graph model families. The first is the Erdős–Rényi graph G⁡(n,c/n)G(n,c/n), which is sparse and has degrees concentrated about their mean; it represents limited and roughly homogeneous interference. The second is the Barabási–Albert graph, whose degree distribution is heavy-tailed and contains a few high-degree hubs; it represents the heterogeneous interference common in social and economic networks. We use n=2000n=2000 units in the Erdős–Rényi experiments and n=3000n=3000 in the Barabási–Albert experiment.

The exposure mapping is the fraction of treated neighbors, ei=di−1​∑j∈Nizje_{i}=d_{i}^{-1}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}, with ei=0e_{i}=0 when di=0d_{i}=0. Potential outcomes follow the decomposition Yi​(z,e)=μi+Ai​(z)+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e)Y_{i}(z,e)=\mu_{i}+A_{i}(z)+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e), with Ai​(z)=αi​zA_{i}(z)=\alpha_{i}z, Bi​(e)=βi​eB_{i}(e)=\beta_{i}e, and Ci​(e)=γi​eC_{i}(e)=\gamma_{i}e. The unit-level coefficients are drawn independently once, with μi∼Unif⁡(−0.2,0.2)\mu_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(-0.2,0.2), αi∼Unif⁡(0.3,0.7)\alpha_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0.3,0.7), βi∼Unif⁡(0.2,0.6)\beta_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0.2,0.6), and γi∼Unif⁡(0,0.4)\gamma_{i}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,0.4), and then held fixed. Thus the response surface is bounded and heterogeneous across units. The interaction coefficients have positive mean, so the direct and expected direct effects differ. The figures focus on three estimands: the direct treatment effect, which contrasts Yi​(1,0)Y_{i}(1,0) and Yi​(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0); the expected direct effect under the Bernoulli allocation policy; and the expected indirect effect under the same policy. Because the treated-neighbor count is binomial conditional on the graph under a Bernoulli design, each target is available in closed form and estimation error is measured against the exact finite-population value.

Each effect is estimated by the corresponding Horvitz–Thompson estimator of Section 4: treatment–exposure weights for the direct treatment effect, fixed own-treatment weights for the expected direct effect, and graph-aware weights for the expected indirect effect. The usual difference-in-means estimator appears separately in Figure 2; it is the ratio form of the own-treatment weighted estimator. We consider two designs: a graph-unaware Bernoulli design with treatment probability one half, used in all but one experiment, and an independent-set design aligned with the direct treatment effect. Each reported error is the root-mean-square error over independent draws of the assignment; Figures 1–3 use Monte Carlo repetitions, while Figure 4 reports the exact probability that the relevant potential outcome is observed at least once in 10410^{4} Bernoulli assignments. The Horvitz–Thompson estimators are design-unbiased by construction, and we confirmed that the empirical bias of each is zero up to Monte Carlo error.

Figure 1 reports the root-mean-square error against the mean interference degree on the Erdős–Rényi graphs; the vertical axis is logarithmic, so a straight line is exponential growth. The direct treatment effect (red circles) follows the inverse-propensity scale for observing Yi​(1,0)Y_{i}(1,0) or Yi​(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0) (the red dashed line, Proposition 20). The expected direct effect (blue squares) is horizontal, as Proposition 23 predicts, and stays near its dependence scale (the blue dashed line). The expected indirect effect (green triangles) rises only polynomially, well below the direct effect. The three estimands use the same graph, the same design, and the same outcomes. The separation is not only asymptotic. At bounded degree the RMSE of both classes decreases at the parametric rate n−1/2n^{-1/2}, but the constant differs sharply: for the direct treatment effect the effective sample size is of order n​p​(1−p)dnp(1-p)^{d}, since only assignments revealing the relevant potential outcomes contribute, whereas the expected direct effect uses every unit and its constant grows only polynomially in the degree. Computed at a single sample size, Figure 1 shows that this gap in constants is already large at the sizes typical of experiments.

Figure 2 follows a single estimator, the difference in means, against two targets as the sample grows. Its error for the expected direct effect (blue) decays as a straight line of slope −1/2-1/2 on the logarithmic axes, the parametric rate; its error for the direct treatment effect (red) flattens at a positive floor, the horizontal dashed line at C¯π\bar{C}_{\pi}. The estimand class, not the estimator, governs consistency: the same estimator is consistent for the effect the design averages over and inconsistent for the fixed-exposure effect on the same data. The decomposition Yi​(z,e)=Ai​(z)+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e)Y_{i}(z,e)=A_{i}(z)+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e) identifies the floor exactly. It is the policy-averaged treatment–exposure interaction C¯π\bar{C}_{\pi}, equal to p​n−1​∑iγip\,n^{-1}\sum_{i}\gamma_{i} in this simulation, and is the part of the response surface that own-treatment contrasts cannot remove; under additivity, Ci≡0C_{i}\equiv 0, the floor vanishes and the difference in means is consistent for the direct effect as well.

Figure 3 illustrates the first route around the exponential barrier for estimating ACEs. The independent-set design treats mutually non-adjacent ego units and holds their neighborhoods at control, so each ego reveals one of the two potential outcomes that define the direct treatment effect, Yi​(1,0)Y_{i}(1,0) or Yi​(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0). On the same Erdős–Rényi graphs as Figure 1, the error under the Bernoulli design (red) grows exponentially in the degree, while the error under the independent-set design (purple) remains nearly flat.

Figure 4 turns to a heavy-tailed Barabási–Albert graph. The direct-effect potential outcome for a high-degree unit is observed with probability that decays exponentially in the unit’s degree, so the inverse propensity of the highest-degree unit exceeds 107010^{70} (left panel) and the probability of seeing the relevant potential outcome at least once in 10410^{4} assignment draws is essentially zero (right panel). The fixed-exposure ACE is not merely expensive to estimate on such graphs; at feasible sample sizes it is effectively non-estimable for the hubs, while the expected direct effect uses every unit. Truncating or stabilizing the extreme inverse-propensity weights can reduce variance, but only by changing the estimator and introducing bias for the fixed finite-population target unless additional modeling assumptions are imposed. Heterogeneity in the degree distribution sharpens the separation rather than softening it: the cost of a fixed-exposure ACE is governed by the exponential moment of the degree distribution, which the hubs dominate.

8 Discussion

For principled causal inference, the potential-outcomes framework keeps three ingredients separate: restrictions on the potential outcomes, the definition of a causal estimand, and the design and estimator used to learn it. Without interference, the first ingredient is a single clean exclusion restriction: each unit has two potential outcomes. Interference is not the negation of that restriction. It is a family of possible restrictions. One has to specify which units’ treatment assignments can affect a given unit’s potential outcome, how those assignments enter the potential outcome, and whether the response surface has additional structure such as additivity, homogeneity, or linearity. The non-parametric decomposition of potential outcomes given in this paper provides a unified language to specify any finite-population model of potential outcomes under interference.

Moreover, without interference there is a single canonical finite-population average treatment effect. With interference there are multiple causal effects of interest, such as direct effects, spillover effects, total effects, and policy effects. We classify estimands under interference into two broad categories: average causal effects, which contrast fixed potential outcomes, and expected causal effects, which average potential outcomes under an allocation policy. This distinction matters because the same name can refer to different functionals of the potential-outcome table. For example, a direct effect may be a fixed contrast holding neighbors’ treatment fixed, as in the direct treatment effect. It may also average over the neighbor treatments generated by an allocation policy, as in the expected direct effect. These estimands coincide under additivity, but not in general.

This perspective also clarifies why several results in the literature that appear to point in different directions are compatible. Partial-interference analyses specify groups and exposure within groups, and the resulting effects are tied to the group-level allocation policy (Hudgens and Halloran, 2008). Exposure-mapping approaches target average causal effects by contrasting fixed treatment–exposure combinations (Aronow and Samii, 2017). Some estimators remain valid under unknown interference because their targets average over the exposure distribution induced by a policy or design; in the terminology of this paper, the average direct effect studied by Sävje et al. (2017) is an expected direct effect. Other approaches recover average causal effects under unknown network structure by imposing outcome-model restrictions; for example, Yu et al. (2022) target a total treatment effect using additivity and linearity. Estimation of these effects is not free. The graph assumption is replaced either by a policy-averaged target or by an outcome-model assumption on the potential outcomes.

The same distinction governs design. Classical graph-unaware designs are often well matched to estimate policy-averaged expected effects, because they generate the exposure distribution being averaged over. They are poorly matched to estimate fixed-exposure average effects when the defining treatment–exposure combinations are rare. In observational studies without interference, positivity requires treatment variation within the covariate strata that define the target comparison. Under interference, the analogous strata are treatment–exposure cells. A Bernoulli design gives abundant information about typical exposure states, but a direct treatment effect ACE may require the atypical cell in which a treated unit has no treated neighbors. Similarly, a total treatment effect ACE may require all-treated and all-control neighborhoods. These cells can have exponentially small probability in the interference degree under classical designs. Fixed-exposure ACEs therefore require either estimand-aligned designs or outcome-model restrictions. Coarsening the spillover boundary can collapse this cost: under the any-treated exposure map the influencer spillover effect is estimated with constant focal propensities by sparse seeding on locally tree-like regular graphs (Section 5.3), while the uncompressed full-exposure versions retain the exponential barrier and need the distance-two design.

The exponential-versus-polynomial gap implies that the estimand and the design cannot be chosen separately. An investigator who targets a fixed-exposure average causal effect but implements a classical design will incur large estimation errors. The estimand and a design that reveals it must be chosen together, at the planning stage. When the design cannot be controlled, as in observational studies, the situation is more severe: average causal effects are then essentially out of reach without strong outcome models or bounded or logarithmic interference degrees, whereas expected causal effects aligned with the assignment mechanism remain estimable under the conditions that make them estimable by design.

A central problem is that the graph and exposure mapping are rarely known at the design stage. If the specified graph and exposure mapping are correct, a fixed-exposure average causal effect is a contrast on the reduced potential outcomes. If the exposure mapping is misspecified, the same contrast may average over assignment features that the mapping omits; this distinction between a target defined under a working exposure mapping and the corresponding target in the full Table of Science is emphasized by Sävje (2024). The same issue arises for the interference graph. If the graph omits relevant treatment coordinates, a fixed-exposure contrast in the reduced representation averages over those omitted coordinates in the full Table of Science. It is then no longer the original fixed-exposure ACE, but a coarsened estimand defined by the misspecified representation. This is not only a matter of bias in an estimator. The target itself has changed.

Several problems follow. Experiments should be designed so that conclusions are stable to plausible changes in the interference graph and exposure mapping. When network data, pretreatment covariates, or repeated experiments are used to learn these objects, the uncertainty in that learning step should enter the final inference. Variance estimation must account for randomization dependence and interference dependence at the same time. Model-assisted estimators add another layer: the fitted response model can reduce variance or recover information from nuisance potential outcomes, but its use must be separated from the design-based correction it supports. These are the questions that arise after the estimand, the interference model, and the design have been put in the same language.

Appendix A Additional examples and extensions for Section 2

A.1 Asymmetric and bipartite interference

While many models assume symmetric interference, interference may be directional. For instance, in social hierarchies or upstream–downstream systems, the treatment of one unit can affect another without a reciprocal effect. In these cases, the in-degree represents a unit’s exposure to external interference, while the out-degree measures that unit’s reach within the network.

The framework also extends to bipartite interference. In such cases, the graph G=(U∪V,E)G=(U\cup V,E) consists of a set of treatment units UU and outcome units VV, where edges only exist from UU to VV. This structure is useful when the units being treated differ from the units whose outcomes are measured, as in environmental and service-provider settings (Zigler and Papadogeorgou, 2021).

A.2 Vector-valued and continuous exposures

The exposure function may be multidimensional. For example, in a social network one may use

ei=(number of treated friends,number of treated friends-of-friends).e_{i}=\big(\text{number of treated friends},\ \text{number of treated friends-of-friends}\big).

In settings where interference is governed by physical proximity, the exposure mapping can be defined as a continuous function of geographic distance. For example, NiN_{i} can represent all units within a relevant radius, with

ei=∑j∈NiK⁡(ρi​j,ϕ)​zj,e_{i}=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}K(\rho_{ij};\phi)z_{j},

where ρi​j\rho_{ij} is the distance between units ii and jj, and K⁡(⋅)K(\cdot) is a kernel function parameterized by ϕ\phi (Giffin et al., 2023).

A.3 Nonlinear and threshold outcome restrictions

The decomposition in Theorem 2 also accommodates nonlinear restrictions on the spillover function BiB_{i} and the interaction function CiC_{i}. For example, under additivity (Ci=0C_{i}=0), one may posit a concave interference function such as Bi​(ei)=γ​log⁡(1+ei)B_{i}(e_{i})=\gamma\log(1+e_{i}), a convex function such as Bi​(ei)=γ​ei2B_{i}(e_{i})=\gamma e_{i}^{2}, or a sigmoidal function

Yi​(zi,ei)=αi+βi​zi+L1+exp⁡{−k⁡(ei−e0)}.Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+\frac{L}{1+\exp\{-k(e_{i}-e_{0})\}}.

Such restrictions arise in settings where the first few treated neighbors have large effects, or where spillovers occur only after a threshold has been reached (Aral and Walker, 2011; Leskovec et al., 2007; De Giorgi et al., 2010).

Threshold and contagion models can be represented by binary exposure mappings such as

ei=𝕀⁡(∑j∈Nizj≥K),e_{i}=\mathbb{I}\left(\sum_{j\in N_{i}}z_{j}\geq K\right),

which are often used in models of collective behavior and complex contagion (Granovetter, 1978; Centola, 2010). Additional structural restrictions can then be imposed on Bi​(ei)B_{i}(e_{i}) and Ci​(ei)C_{i}(e_{i}) depending on whether individual treatment and exposure are substitutes, complements, or interact in some other way.

A.4 Non-anonymous exposure

In non-anonymous interference, the effect of neighbors’ treatments depends on their identities or covariates. One example is

ei=∑j∈Niw⁡(Xj)​zj,e_{i}=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}w(X_{j})z_{j},

where XjX_{j} are neighbor attributes. The potential outcome can then be written as

Yi​(zi,ei)=αi+βi​zi+Bi​(∑j∈Niw⁡(Xj)​zj)+zi​Ci​(∑j∈Niw⁡(Xj)​zj).Y_{i}(z_{i},e_{i})=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z_{i}+B_{i}\left(\sum_{j\in N_{i}}w(X_{j})z_{j}\right)+z_{i}C_{i}\left(\sum_{j\in N_{i}}w(X_{j})z_{j}\right).

This includes weighted and spatial exposure mappings, including environmental settings where exposure depends on distance or direction (Zigler et al., 2012; Patacchini et al., 2017; Adhikari and Zheleva, 2025).

Thus Yi​(z,e)=Ai​(z)+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e)Y_{i}(z,e)=A_{i}(z)+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e) for every zz and ee.

C.1 Mixed causal effects: EIC, EIT, and ETE

Mixed causal effects contrast expected potential outcomes under a policy against fixed baseline responses. They can be viewed as expected analogues of the ACE indirect effects.

Expected exposure effects.

(C.2)

Expected total effect.

The expected total effect compares the expectation under full treatment to the baseline condition:

τETE​(𝒬)=1n​∑i=1n∑e∈ℰ(Yi​(1,e)−Yi​(0,0))​P𝒬​(Ei=e)=1n​∑iμi​(1,𝒬)−1n​∑iYi​(0,0).\tau_{\mathrm{ETE}}(\mathcal{Q})\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}\Big(Y_{i}(1,e)-Y_{i}(0,0)\Big)\,P_{\mathcal{Q}}(E_{i}=e)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mu_{i}(1;\mathcal{Q})-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}Y_{i}(0,0). C.2 Proof of Proposition 12

Restatement.

Under the non-parametric linear representation of Theorem 2,

Yi​(z,e)=αi+βi​z+Bi​(e)+z​Ci​(e),Bi​(0)=Ci​(0)=0,Y_{i}(z,e)=\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}z+B_{i}(e)+zC_{i}(e),\qquad B_{i}(0)=C_{i}(0)=0,

the ACEs and ECEs have the representations stated in Proposition 12.

Proof.

For the fixed-exposure effects, substitute the representation into each contrast. The direct treatment effect is

Yi​(1,0)−Yi​(0,0)={αi+βi+Bi​(0)+Ci​(0)}−{αi+Bi​(0)}=βi.Y_{i}(1,0)-Y_{i}(0,0)=\{\alpha_{i}+\beta_{i}+B_{i}(0)+C_{i}(0)\}-\{\alpha_{i}+B_{i}(0)\}=\beta_{i}.

Similarly,

Yi​(0,e)−Yi​(0,0)=Bi​(e),Yi​(1,e)−Yi​(1,0)=Bi​(e)+Ci​(e),Y_{i}(0,e)-Y_{i}(0,0)=B_{i}(e),\qquad Y_{i}(1,e)-Y_{i}(1,0)=B_{i}(e)+C_{i}(e),

and

Yi​(1,1)−Yi​(0,0)=βi+Bi​(1)+Ci​(1).Y_{i}(1,1)-Y_{i}(0,0)=\beta_{i}+B_{i}(1)+C_{i}(1).

Averaging these identities over ii gives the ACE formulas.

For the expected effects, take expectations with respect to the exposure distribution induced by the allocation policy. Since

Yi​(1,Ei)−Yi​(0,Ei)=βi+Ci​(Ei),Y_{i}(1,E_{i})-Y_{i}(0,E_{i})=\beta_{i}+C_{i}(E_{i}),

we have

τEDE​(𝒬)=1n​∑iβi+1n​∑i𝔼𝒬​[Ci​(Ei)].\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[C_{i}(E_{i})].

The remaining three formulas follow from

Yi​(0,Ei)−Yi​(0,0)=Bi​(Ei),Y_{i}(0,E_{i})-Y_{i}(0,0)=B_{i}(E_{i}),
Yi​(1,Ei)−Yi​(1,0)=Bi​(Ei)+Ci​(Ei),Y_{i}(1,E_{i})-Y_{i}(1,0)=B_{i}(E_{i})+C_{i}(E_{i}),

and

Yi​(1,Ei)−Yi​(0,0)=βi+Bi​(Ei)+Ci​(Ei).Y_{i}(1,E_{i})-Y_{i}(0,0)=\beta_{i}+B_{i}(E_{i})+C_{i}(E_{i}).

∎

C.3 Proof of Proposition 14

Restatement.

The total treatment effect satisfies

τTTE=τDTE+τIET.\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}.

Under additivity, Ci​(e)=0C_{i}(e)=0 for all i,ei,e, so

τTTE=τDTE+τIET=τDTE+τIEC.\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}.
Proof.

By Proposition 12,

τTTE=1n​∑i{βi+Bi​(1)+Ci​(1)},\tau_{\mathrm{TTE}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{\beta_{i}+B_{i}(1)+C_{i}(1)\},

while

τDTE+τIET=1n​∑iβi+1n​∑i{Bi​(1)+Ci​(1)}.\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\{B_{i}(1)+C_{i}(1)\}.

The two expressions are equal. If Ci​(e)=0C_{i}(e)=0 for all i,ei,e, then τIET=τIEC\tau_{\mathrm{IET}}=\tau_{\mathrm{IEC}}, which gives the additive form. ∎

C.4 Proof of Proposition 35

Restatement.

For any allocation policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q},

τETE​(𝒬)=τEDE​(𝒬)+τEIC​(𝒬)=τDTE+τEIT​(𝒬).\tau_{\mathrm{ETE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})+\tau_{\mathrm{EIC}}(\mathcal{Q})=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{EIT}}(\mathcal{Q}).
Proof.

Using the notation of Proposition 12,

τETE​(𝒬)=1n​∑iβi+B¯𝒬+C¯𝒬.\tau_{\mathrm{ETE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}}+\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

Also,

τEDE​(𝒬)+τEIC​(𝒬)={1n​∑iβi+C¯𝒬}+B¯𝒬,\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})+\tau_{\mathrm{EIC}}(\mathcal{Q})=\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}\right\}+\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}},

and

τDTE+τEIT​(𝒬)=1n​∑iβi+B¯𝒬+C¯𝒬.\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}+\tau_{\mathrm{EIT}}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}+\bar{B}_{\mathcal{Q}}+\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}.

Both expressions equal τETE​(𝒬)\tau_{\mathrm{ETE}}(\mathcal{Q}). ∎

C.5 Proof of Corollary 13

Restatement.

Under additivity of the causal response surface, τEDE​(𝒬)=τDTE\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}} for every allocation policy 𝒬\mathcal{Q}.

Proof.

Under additivity, Ci​(e)=0C_{i}(e)=0 for all units and exposure levels. Therefore C¯𝒬=n−1​∑i𝔼𝒬​[Ci​(Ei)]=0\bar{C}_{\mathcal{Q}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{Q}}[C_{i}(E_{i})]=0, and Proposition 12 gives

τEDE​(𝒬)=1n​∑iβi=τDTE.\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\beta_{i}=\tau_{\mathrm{DTE}}.

∎

C.6 Proof of Proposition 11

Restatement.

Under a Bernoulli assignment, the exposure mapping versions of EDE and EIE decompose the derivative of the expected population outcome:

τTPE​(π)=τEDE​(π)+τEIE​(π).\tau_{\text{TPE}}(\pi)=\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\pi)+\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi).
Proof.

Let the treatment vector be 𝐙=(Z1,…,Zn)\mathbf{Z}=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}), where Zi∼Bernoulli​(πi)Z_{i}\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\pi_{i}) are independent. Let ei=f⁡(𝐙Ni)e_{i}=f(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}}) be the exposure mapping for unit ii. The expected population outcome under the policy π=(π1,…,πn)\pi=(\pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{n}) is

μ⁡(π)=1n​∑i=1n𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei)].\mu(\pi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i})].

By the multivariate chain rule,

τTPE​(π)=∑j=1n∂∂πj​μ​(π)=1n​∑i=1n{∂∂πi​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei)]+∑j∈Ni∂∂πj​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei)]},\tau_{\mathrm{TPE}}(\pi)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi_{j}}\mu(\pi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi_{i}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i})]+\sum_{j\in N_{i}}\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi_{j}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i})]\right\},

where the partial derivative is zero for j∉Ni∪{i}j\notin N_{i}\cup\{i\}.

For the own-treatment derivative, the independence of ZiZ_{i} from eie_{i} under Bernoulli assignment gives

∂∂πi​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei)]=𝔼π​[Yi​(1,ei)−Yi​(0,ei)].\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi_{i}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i})]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[Y_{i}(1,e_{i})-Y_{i}(0,e_{i})\right].

Averaging over ii gives τEDE​(π)\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\pi).

For j∈Nij\in N_{i}, define

ei+j=ei​(ZNi∖j,zj=1),ei−j=ei​(ZNi∖j,zj=0).e_{i}^{+j}=e_{i}(Z_{N_{i}\setminus j},z_{j}=1),\qquad e_{i}^{-j}=e_{i}(Z_{N_{i}\setminus j},z_{j}=0).

Again using the product structure of the Bernoulli design,

∂∂πj​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei)]=𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,ei+j)−Yi​(Zi,ei−j)].\frac{\partial}{\partial\pi_{j}}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i})]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i}^{+j})-Y_{i}(Z_{i},e_{i}^{-j})\right].

Summing over j∈Nij\in N_{i} and averaging over ii gives τEIE​(π)\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi). Combining the own-treatment and neighbor-treatment terms proves

τTPE​(π)=τEDE​(π)+τEIE​(π).\tau_{\mathrm{TPE}}(\pi)=\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\pi)+\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi).

∎

C.7 Symmetric exposure mappings

Proposition 36 (EIE under symmetric exposure).

Suppose the assignment is Bernoulli with common probability π\pi, and suppose the exposure mapping is symmetric. If

ei​(𝐙Ni)=∑j∈NiZj,di=|Ni|,e_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}})=\sum_{j\in N_{i}}Z_{j},\qquad d_{i}=|N_{i}|,

then the expected indirect effect can be written as

τEIE​(π)=1n​∑i=1ndi​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,E~i+1)−Yi​(Zi,E~i)],\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[Y_{i}(Z_{i},\widetilde{E}_{i}+1)-Y_{i}(Z_{i},\widetilde{E}_{i})\right],

where E~i\widetilde{E}_{i} is the exposure generated by the remaining di−1d_{i}-1 neighbors. If instead

ei​(𝐙Ni)=1di​∑j∈NiZj,e_{i}(\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}})=\frac{1}{d_{i}}\sum_{j\in N_{i}}Z_{j},

then

τEIE​(π)=1n​∑i=1ndi​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,E~i+1di)−Yi​(Zi,E~i)],\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[Y_{i}\left(Z_{i},\widetilde{E}_{i}+\frac{1}{d_{i}}\right)-Y_{i}\left(Z_{i},\widetilde{E}_{i}\right)\right],

where E~i\widetilde{E}_{i} is the fractional exposure generated by the remaining di−1d_{i}-1 neighbors.

Proof.

For the count exposure, fix ii and j∈Nij\in N_{i}. Since the Bernoulli design has a common treatment probability and the exposure mapping is symmetric, the distribution of the exposure generated by Ni∖{j}N_{i}\setminus\{j\} is the same for every neighbor jj. Moreover,

ei+j=E~i+1,ei−j=E~i.e_{i}^{+j}=\widetilde{E}_{i}+1,\qquad e_{i}^{-j}=\widetilde{E}_{i}.

Substituting these two expressions into the definition of τEIE​(π)\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi) and summing the identical neighbor contributions over j∈Nij\in N_{i} gives

τEIE​(π)=1n​∑i=1ndi​𝔼π​[Yi​(Zi,E~i+1)−Yi​(Zi,E~i)].\tau_{\mathrm{EIE}}(\pi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}d_{i}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[Y_{i}(Z_{i},\widetilde{E}_{i}+1)-Y_{i}(Z_{i},\widetilde{E}_{i})\right].

For fractional exposure, changing ZjZ_{j} from zero to one increases exposure by 1/di1/d_{i}. Thus

ei+j=E~i+1di,ei−j=E~i,e_{i}^{+j}=\widetilde{E}_{i}+\frac{1}{d_{i}},\qquad e_{i}^{-j}=\widetilde{E}_{i},

and the same averaging argument gives the second formula. ∎

Appendix D Proofs for Section 4

D.1 Proof of Lemma 18

Proof.

If there is no dependence-graph edge between two disjoint vertex sets AA and BB, then 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\emptyset for every i∈Ai\in A and j∈Bj\in B. Hence the assignment coordinates in ∪i∈A𝒞i\cup_{i\in A}\mathcal{C}_{i} are disjoint from the assignment coordinates in ∪j∈B𝒞j\cup_{j\in B}\mathcal{C}_{j}. Since treatment assignments are mutually independent, the two assignment subvectors are independent. Because each XiX_{i} is a function of 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}, the collections {Xi:i∈A}\{X_{i}:i\in A\} and {Xj:j∈B}\{X_{j}:j\in B\} are independent. Thus the graph defined by ci​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅}c_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\} is a valid dependence graph.

Now suppose the interference graph is undirected. Then 𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset if and only if ii and jj are at graph distance at most two. Hence ci=|B2​(i)|−1c_{i}=|B_{2}(i)|-1. Since every neighbor of ii lies in B2​(i)B_{2}(i), ci≥dic_{i}\geq d_{i}, and averaging gives cavg≥d¯c_{\mathrm{avg}}\geq\bar{d}. For the upper bound, the vertices within graph distance at most two from ii, excluding ii, consist of the did_{i} neighbors of ii and the additional vertices reached through those neighbors. Thus

ci≤di+∑ℓ∈Ni(dℓ−1)=∑ℓ∈Nidℓ.c_{i}\leq d_{i}+\sum_{\ell\in N_{i}}(d_{\ell}-1)=\sum_{\ell\in N_{i}}d_{\ell}.

Averaging over ii and using the symmetry of the undirected graph gives

cavg≤1n​∑i=1n∑ℓ∈Nidℓ=1n​∑ℓ=1ndℓ2.c_{\mathrm{avg}}\leq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\in N_{i}}d_{\ell}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}d_{\ell}^{2}.

The bound cavg≤n−1c_{\mathrm{avg}}\leq n-1 is immediate because each unit has at most n−1n-1 other units in its dependence neighborhood. ∎

D.2 A generic design-dependence bound

The following auxiliary result separates dependence generated by overlapping assignment coordinates from dependence induced by the randomization design, using the design-dependence coefficient in Definition 19.

Proposition 37 (Interference and design dependence bound).

Consider a generic design-based estimator of the form

Ψ^=1n​∑i=1nψi​(𝐙),\hat{\Psi}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),

ℓi​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅},i≠j.\ell_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\},\qquad i\neq j.

B2,n2=1n​∑i=1nBi2,B_{2,n}^{2}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}B_{i}^{2},
LB=1n​∑i=1n∑j≠iℓi​j​Bi​Bj,L_{B}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}\ell_{ij}B_{i}B_{j},

and

RB=1n​∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ℓi​j)​ρi​jP​Bi​Bj.R_{B}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-\ell_{ij})\rho_{ij}^{P}B_{i}B_{j}.

Then, under an arbitrary design PP,

VarP⁡(1n​∑i=1nψi​(𝐙))≤1n​{B2,n2+LB+RB}.\operatorname{Var}_{P}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\right)\leq\frac{1}{n}\{B_{2,n}^{2}+L_{B}+R_{B}\}.

Write Ψ^=n−1​∑iψi​(𝐙)\hat{\Psi}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}). The variance expansion gives

VarP⁡(Ψ^)=1n2​[∑iVarP⁡{ψi​(𝐙)}+∑i∑j≠iCovP⁡{ψi​(𝐙),ψj​(𝐙)}].\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\hat{\Psi})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[\sum_{i}\operatorname{Var}_{P}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\operatorname{Cov}_{P}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})\}\right].

Since |ψi|≤Bi|\psi_{i}|\leq B_{i}, VarP⁡(ψi)≤Bi2\operatorname{Var}_{P}(\psi_{i})\leq B_{i}^{2}. If ℓi​j=1\ell_{ij}=1, then

|CovP⁡{ψi​(𝐙),ψj​(𝐙)}|≤𝔼P​|ψi​(𝐙)​ψj​(𝐙)|≤Bi​Bj.\left|\operatorname{Cov}_{P}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})\}\right|\leq\mathbb{E}_{P}|\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq B_{i}B_{j}.

If ℓi​j=0\ell_{ij}=0, then 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\emptyset. When Bi​Bj>0B_{i}B_{j}>0, set f⁡(𝐙𝒞i)=ψi​(𝐙)/Bif(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}})=\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})/B_{i} and g⁡(𝐙𝒞j)=ψj​(𝐙)/Bjg(\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{j}})=\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})/B_{j}. If Bi​Bj=0B_{i}B_{j}=0, the same bound is immediate. Substituting these three bounds into the variance expansion proves the result. ∎

D.3 Residual design dependence under complete randomization

The residual design-dependence term can be bounded explicitly for complete randomization. Suppose the design assigns exactly mm of the nn units to treatment. If A,B⊆{1,…,n}A,B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\} are disjoint assignment-coordinate sets with |A|=a|A|=a and |B|=b|B|=b, then

ρP​(A,B)≤C​min⁡{1,a​bn−a−b},\rho_{P}(A,B)\leq C\min\left\{1,\frac{ab}{n-a-b}\right\},

for a universal constant CC, whenever a+b<na+b<n. Consequently, for local HT/IPW estimators whose iith summand depends on 𝒞i={i}∪Ni\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{i\}\cup N_{i},

ravg≤Cn​∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​min⁡{1,|𝒞i|​|𝒞j|n−|𝒞i|−|𝒞j|}.r_{\mathrm{avg}}\leq\frac{C}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})\min\left\{1,\frac{|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\,|\mathcal{C}_{j}|}{n-|\mathcal{C}_{i}|-|\mathcal{C}_{j}|}\right\}.

In particular, if maxi⁡|𝒞i|≤n/4\max_{i}|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\leq n/4, then

ravg≤Cn2​∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​|𝒞i|​|𝒞j|≤C​(1n​∑i=1n|𝒞i|)2.r_{\mathrm{avg}}\leq\frac{C}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\,|\mathcal{C}_{j}|\leq C\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\mathcal{C}_{i}|\right)^{2}.

Thus on a dd-regular local interference graph, ravg=O⁡(d2)r_{\mathrm{avg}}=O(d^{2}), matching the order of cavg≍d2c_{\mathrm{avg}}\asymp d^{2}. For bounded-degree graphs, ravg=O⁡(1)r_{\mathrm{avg}}=O(1), so the residual design-dependence contribution H​ravg/nH\sqrt{r_{\mathrm{avg}}/n} has the same n−1/2n^{-1/2} scaling as the Bernoulli dependence term, up to the relevant propensity scale HH.

Proof.

It suffices to bound the dependence between two disjoint subvectors. For a fixed configuration xAx_{A} with s=∑ℓ∈Axℓs=\sum_{\ell\in A}x_{\ell}, the conditional distribution of 𝐙B\mathbf{Z}_{B} under complete randomization is sampling without replacement from a population of size n−an-a containing m−sm-s treated labels. The marginal distribution of 𝐙B\mathbf{Z}_{B} is sampling without replacement from a population of size nn containing mm treated labels.

Couple the two draws sequentially over the bb coordinates in BB. After k<bk<b coordinates in BB have been exposed and rr treated labels have appeared among them, the two conditional probabilities that the next coordinate is treated are

m−s−rn−a−kandm−rn−k.\frac{m-s-r}{n-a-k}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{m-r}{n-k}.

Their absolute difference is at most C​a/(n−a−b)Ca/(n-a-b), uniformly over admissible s,r,ks,r,k. For any ‖g‖∞≤1\|g\|_{\infty}\leq 1, the difference between the conditional and marginal expectations of g⁡(𝐙B)g(\mathbf{Z}_{B}) is at most twice this total variation distance. Taking the supremum also over ‖f‖∞≤1\|f\|_{\infty}\leq 1 gives the displayed bound for ρP​(A,B)\rho_{P}(A,B).

The simplified bound follows from |𝒞i|+|𝒞j|≤n/2|\mathcal{C}_{i}|+|\mathcal{C}_{j}|\leq n/2, and the final regular and bounded-degree statements follow by setting |𝒞i|=d+1|\mathcal{C}_{i}|=d+1 or maxi⁡|𝒞i|=O⁡(1)\max_{i}|\mathcal{C}_{i}|=O(1). ∎

|Cov⁡(XiA​C​E,XjA​C​E)|≤M2​ρi​j​Hi​Hj.|\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i}^{ACE},X_{j}^{ACE})|\leq M^{2}\rho_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}.

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T​(d+,d−)}\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}(d^{+},d^{-})\} =1n2​{∑i=1nVar⁡(XiA​C​E)+∑i=1n∑j≠iCov⁡(XiA​C​E,XjA​C​E)}\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(X_{i}^{ACE})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}\operatorname{Cov}(X_{i}^{ACE},X_{j}^{ACE})\right\}
≤M2n2​{∑i=1nHi+∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j​Hi​Hj+∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​ρi​j​Hi​Hj}.\displaystyle\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})\rho_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}\right\}.

If Hi≤HH_{i}\leq H for all ii, this becomes

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T​(d+,d−)}\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}(d^{+},d^{-})\} ≤M2n2​{n​H+H2​∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j+H2​∑i=1n∑j≠i(1−ci​j)​ρi​j}\displaystyle\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{nH+H^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}+H^{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}(1-c_{ij})\rho_{ij}\right\}
=M2​{Hn+H2​cavg+ravgn}.\displaystyle=M^{2}\left\{\frac{H}{n}+H^{2}\frac{c_{\mathrm{avg}}+r_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}\right\}.

∎
