D.7 Weighted dependence bound for graph-aware ECEs

Definition 38 (Weighted summand and dependence complexity).

Write hi​(𝐙)=hi+​(𝐙)−hi−​(𝐙)h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=h_{i}^{+}(\mathbf{Z})-h_{i}^{-}(\mathbf{Z}) and ψi​(𝐙)=hi​(𝐙)​Yi​{Di​(𝐙)}\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})Y_{i}\{D_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}. For the canonical ECE estimator τ^h=n−1​∑iψi​(𝐙)\hat{\tau}_{h}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}), define

ωi​j​(Y)=Cov⁡{ψi​(𝐙),ψj​(𝐙)},i≠j,\omega_{ij}(Y)=\operatorname{Cov}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})\},\qquad i\neq j,

and

Γh​(M)=sup|Y|≤M[∑i=1nVar⁡{ψi​(𝐙)}+∑i=1n∑j≠iωi​j​(Y)].\Gamma_{h}(M)=\sup_{|Y|\leq M}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}\omega_{ij}(Y)\right].

The supremum is over all bounded potential-outcome tables satisfying |Yi​(𝐳)|≤M|Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})|\leq M.

Proposition 39 (Weighted dependence bound for graph-aware ECEs).

Assume independent Bernoulli assignment. Suppose the potential outcomes satisfy neighborhood interference with known neighborhoods NiN_{i}, and suppose hi​(𝐙)h_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) depends only on 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}. Then a valid dependence graph for ψi​(𝐙)=hi​(𝐙)​Yi​(𝐙)\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) is given by

ci​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅},i≠j.c_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\},\qquad i\neq j.

Moreover,

sup|Y|≤MVar⁡(τ^h)=Γh​(M)n2.\sup_{|Y|\leq M}\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{h})=\frac{\Gamma_{h}(M)}{n^{2}}.

In particular, if |hi​(𝐙)|≤Hi|h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq H_{i}, then

Var⁡(τ^h)≤M2n2​{∑i=1nHi2+∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j​Hi​Hj}.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{h})\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}\right\}.

This result separates two roles of the dependence graph. The unweighted graph gives a conservative upper bound by replacing every nonzero covariance by its maximal possible size. The sharper object is the weighted dependence complexity Γh​(M)\Gamma_{h}(M), which keeps the covariance weights induced by the design contrast and the potential-outcome table.

D.8 Proof of Proposition 39

Restatement.

Assume independent Bernoulli assignment. Suppose the potential outcomes satisfy neighborhood interference with known neighborhoods NiN_{i}, and suppose hi​(𝐙)h_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) depends only on 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}, where 𝒞i={i}∪Ni\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{i\}\cup N_{i}. Then a valid dependence graph for ψi​(𝐙)=hi​(𝐙)​Yi​(𝐙)\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) is given by

ci​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅},i≠j.c_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\},\qquad i\neq j.

Moreover,

sup|Y|≤MVar⁡(τ^h)=Γh​(M)n2.\sup_{|Y|\leq M}\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{h})=\frac{\Gamma_{h}(M)}{n^{2}}.

If |hi​(𝐙)|≤Hi|h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq H_{i}, then

Var⁡(τ^h)≤M2n2​{∑i=1nHi2+∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j​Hi​Hj}.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{h})\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}H_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}\right\}.
Proof.

By neighborhood interference, Yi​(𝐙)Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) is a function only of 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}. By assumption, hi​(𝐙)h_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) is also a function only of 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}. Hence

ψi​(𝐙)=hi​(𝐙)​Yi​(𝐙)\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})=h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z})

is a function only of 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}. If 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\emptyset, then 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}} and 𝐙𝒞j\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{j}} are independent under independent Bernoulli assignment. Therefore ψi​(𝐙)\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}) and ψj​(𝐙)\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z}) are independent. The graph with edge indicators ci​j=𝟙{𝒞i∩𝒞j≠∅}c_{ij}=\mathds{1}\{\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}\neq\emptyset\} is therefore a valid dependence graph.

For a fixed potential-outcome table YY,

τ^h=1n​∑i=1nψi​(𝐙),\hat{\tau}_{h}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),

so

Var⁡(τ^h)=1n2​[∑i=1nVar⁡{ψi​(𝐙)}+∑i=1n∑j≠iCov⁡{ψi​(𝐙),ψj​(𝐙)}].\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{h})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}\operatorname{Cov}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})\}\right].

Taking the supremum over all bounded potential-outcome tables gives

sup|Y|≤MVar⁡(τ^h)=Γh​(M)n2\sup_{|Y|\leq M}\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{h})=\frac{\Gamma_{h}(M)}{n^{2}}

by Definition 38.

Finally, if |Yi​(𝐙)|≤M|Y_{i}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq M and |hi​(𝐙)|≤Hi|h_{i}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq H_{i}, then |ψi​(𝐙)|≤M​Hi|\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq MH_{i}. Thus

Var⁡{ψi​(𝐙)}≤M2​Hi2.\operatorname{Var}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z})\}\leq M^{2}H_{i}^{2}.

If ci​j=0c_{ij}=0, then ψi\psi_{i} and ψj\psi_{j} are independent and the covariance is zero. If ci​j=1c_{ij}=1, then Cauchy–Schwarz gives

|Cov⁡{ψi​(𝐙),ψj​(𝐙)}|≤{Var⁡(ψi)​Var⁡(ψj)}1/2≤M2​Hi​Hj.|\operatorname{Cov}\{\psi_{i}(\mathbf{Z}),\psi_{j}(\mathbf{Z})\}|\leq\{\operatorname{Var}(\psi_{i})\operatorname{Var}(\psi_{j})\}^{1/2}\leq M^{2}H_{i}H_{j}.

Substituting these bounds into the variance expansion gives the stated inequality. ∎

D.9 Proof of Proposition 23

Restatement.

Assume the true potential outcomes satisfy neighborhood interference with neighborhoods NiN_{i}. Assume Bernoulli assignment with treatment probabilities bounded away from zero and one, let 𝒬p\mathcal{Q}_{p} denote this Bernoulli allocation policy, and assume sup𝐳|Yi​(𝐳)|≤M\sup_{\mathbf{z}}|Y_{i}(\mathbf{z})|\leq M. Then τ^EDEH​T\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT} is design-unbiased for τEDE​(𝒬p)\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q}_{p}), and

VarPn⁡(τ^EDEH​T)≤Cp​M2​1+cavgn.\operatorname{Var}_{P_{n}}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT})\leq C_{p}M^{2}\frac{1+c_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}.

In particular, τ^EDEH​T\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT} is design-MSE consistent if cavg=o⁡(n)c_{\mathrm{avg}}=o(n).

Proof.

Write the estimator as n−1​∑iXin^{-1}\sum_{i}X_{i}, where

Xi=Yio​b​s​{Zi/pi−(1−Zi)/(1−pi)}.X_{i}=Y_{i}^{obs}\left\{Z_{i}/p_{i}-(1-Z_{i})/(1-p_{i})\right\}.

First condition on Z−iZ_{-i}. Since the assignment is Bernoulli, ZiZ_{i} is independent of Z−iZ_{-i}, and hence

𝔼⁡(Xi∣Z−i)=Yi​(1,Z−i)−Yi​(0,Z−i).\mathbb{E}(X_{i}\mid Z_{-i})=Y_{i}(1,Z_{-i})-Y_{i}(0,Z_{-i}).

Taking expectations over Z−iZ_{-i} gives

𝔼⁡(τ^EDEH​T)=1n​∑i=1n{𝔼⁡[Yi​(1,Z−i)]−𝔼⁡[Yi​(0,Z−i)]}=τEDE​(𝒬p).\mathbb{E}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left\{\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(1,Z_{-i})]-\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}(0,Z_{-i})]\right\}=\tau_{\mathrm{EDE}}(\mathcal{Q}_{p}).

The boundedness of the potential outcomes and the positivity of the treatment probabilities imply |Xi|≤Cp​M|X_{i}|\leq C_{p}M. If 𝒞i∩𝒞j=∅\mathcal{C}_{i}\cap\mathcal{C}_{j}=\emptyset, then XiX_{i} and XjX_{j} depend on disjoint sets of independent treatment assignments and are therefore independent. Thus only pairs with ci​j=1c_{ij}=1 contribute to the covariance sum. This gives

Var⁡(τ^EDEH​T)≤Cp​M2n2​(n+∑i∑j≠ici​j)=Cp​M2​1+cavgn.\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT})\leq\frac{C_{p}M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left(n+\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}\right)=C_{p}M^{2}\frac{1+c_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}.

∎

D.10 Proof of Corollary 24

Restatement.

|hiEIE,G​(𝐙)|≤Cp​di.|h_{i}^{\mathrm{EIE},G}(\mathbf{Z})|\leq C_{p}d_{i}.

Moreover hiEIE,G​(𝐙)h_{i}^{\mathrm{EIE},G}(\mathbf{Z}) depends only on 𝐙Ni\mathbf{Z}_{N_{i}}, and hence on 𝐙𝒞i\mathbf{Z}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}. Proposition 39, with Hi=Cp​diH_{i}=C_{p}d_{i}, gives

which gives the final display. ∎

D.11 Heterogeneous ACE/ECE comparison under classical designs

The DTE/EDE comparison of Section 4.3 extends to arbitrary heterogeneous degree sequences, where it is governed by two graph functionals. For a fixed-exposure ACE, the relevant scale is the inverse propensity-score moment

𝒜n​(d+)=1n2​∑i=1nπi​(di+)−1;\mathcal{A}_{n}(d^{+})=\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}(d_{i}^{+})^{-1};

for the direct-effect entry (1,0Ni)(1,0_{N_{i}}) under Bernoulli assignment, πi​(1,0Ni)=p​(1−p)di\pi_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}})=p(1-p)^{d_{i}}, so 𝒜n​(1,0)≍n−2​∑iexp⁡(γ​di)\mathcal{A}_{n}(1,0)\asymp n^{-2}\sum_{i}\exp(\gamma d_{i}) is an exponential moment of the degree sequence. For the EDE under the same design, the relevant scale is the average dependence degree, ℬn=cavg/n\mathcal{B}_{n}=c_{\mathrm{avg}}/n.

The comparison is design-specific. It applies to classical designs such as Bernoulli assignment, and complete randomization with a fixed treatment fraction has the same exponential propensity-score behavior for local fixed-exposure combinations, up to finite-population corrections. It does not rule out designs that are constructed to increase the propensity scores of the ACE target combinations, such as the independent-set designs.

The table is meant to show why a single average degree condition is not adequate for heterogeneous graphs. By Jensen’s inequality,

1n​∑i=1nexp⁡(γ​di)≥exp⁡(γ​d¯),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\gamma d_{i})\geq\exp(\gamma\bar{d}),

so large average degree is enough to make the ACE inverse-propensity scale large. However, small average degree is not sufficient to make ACE estimation easy, because hubs can dominate the exponential moment. For EDE estimation, average degree is also not the right quantity: a star graph has d¯=O⁡(1)\bar{d}=O(1) but cavg≍nc_{\mathrm{avg}}\asymp n.

Corollary 40 (Heterogeneous ACE/ECE separation under Bernoulli assignment).

Consider a sequence of undirected interference graphs with degrees di=|Ni|d_{i}=|N_{i}|, and suppose treatment is assigned independently with a common probability pp bounded away from zero and one. For the direct-effect ACE entry (1,0Ni)(1,0_{N_{i}}), there are constants 0<γ1≤γ2<∞0<\gamma_{1}\leq\gamma_{2}<\infty, depending only on pp, such that

1n2​∑i=1nexp⁡(γ1​di)≲1n2​∑i=1nπi​(1,0Ni)−1≲1n2​∑i=1nexp⁡(γ2​di).\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\gamma_{1}d_{i})\lesssim\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}})^{-1}\lesssim\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\gamma_{2}d_{i}).

The canonical ACE Horvitz–Thompson variance is bounded by

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T}≤Cp​M2n2​{∑i=1nexp⁡(γ2​di)+∑i=1n∑j≠ici​j​exp⁡{γ2​(di+dj)}},\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}\}\leq\frac{C_{p}M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp(\gamma_{2}d_{i})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}\exp\{\gamma_{2}(d_{i}+d_{j})\}\right\},

where ci​jc_{ij} is the interference-overlap graph for the ACE summands. By contrast, the canonical EDE Horvitz–Thompson estimator satisfies

Var⁡{τ^EDEH​T}≤Cp​M2​1+cavgn.\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{EDE}}^{HT}\}\leq C_{p}M^{2}\frac{1+c_{\mathrm{avg}}}{n}.

Thus, under the same Bernoulli design and for arbitrary heterogeneous graph sequences, the ACE benchmark involves exponential moments of the degree sequence and their dependence-weighted analogues, whereas the EDE benchmark involves only the average degree of the dependence graph.

The regular-graph comparison of Section 4.3 is recovered as a special case. More generally, Table 3 should be read through the two graph functionals appearing in the corollary: exponential degree moments for ACE target combinations and average dependence degree for EDE importance-weighted estimators.

D.12 Proof of Corollary 40

Restatement.

Proof.

For the direct-effect entry (1,0Ni)(1,0_{N_{i}}) under Bernoulli assignment,

πi​(1,0Ni)=p​(1−p)di.\pi_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}})=p(1-p)^{d_{i}}.

Since pp and 1−p1-p are bounded away from zero and one, there are constants 0<γ1≤γ2<∞0<\gamma_{1}\leq\gamma_{2}<\infty, depending only on pp, such that

exp⁡(γ1​di)≤πi​(1,0Ni)−1≤exp⁡(γ2​di)\exp(\gamma_{1}d_{i})\leq\pi_{i}(1,0_{N_{i}})^{-1}\leq\exp(\gamma_{2}d_{i})

Var⁡{τ^ACEH​T}≤M2n2​{∑iHi+∑i∑j≠ici​j​Hi​Hj}.\operatorname{Var}\{\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{ACE}}^{HT}\}\leq\frac{M^{2}}{n^{2}}\left\{\sum_{i}H_{i}+\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}c_{ij}H_{i}H_{j}\right\}.

D.13 Auxiliary calculation: DTE and TTE table rates

Proposition 41 (DTE and TTE propensities under graph-unaware designs).

Let AiA_{i} denote the assignment coordinates that define the target treatment–exposure combination for unit ii. For arbitrary interference, Ai={1,…,n}A_{i}=\{1,\ldots,n\}, while under neighborhood interference Ai=𝒞i={i}∪NiA_{i}=\mathcal{C}_{i}=\{i\}\cup N_{i}. Write ai=|Ai|a_{i}=|A_{i}|.

  1. (i)

    Suppose the design assigns treatments independently, with ϵ≤P⁡(Zk=1)≤1−ϵ\epsilon\leq P(Z_{k}=1)\leq 1-\epsilon for all kk. Then every fixed assignment pattern on AiA_{i} has probability exp⁡{−Θ⁡(ai)}\exp\{-\Theta(a_{i})\}, with constants depending only on ϵ\epsilon. Consequently, the DTE no-exposure conditions and the TTE full-exposure/no-exposure conditions have inverse propensities exp⁡{Θ⁡(n)}\exp\{\Theta(n)\} under arbitrary interference and exp⁡{Θ⁡(di)}\exp\{\Theta(d_{i})\} under neighborhood interference.

  2. (ii)

    Suppose the design is exchangeable, so that conditional on Tn=∑kZk=mT_{n}=\sum_{k}Z_{k}=m all assignments with mm treated units are equally likely. Assume that, for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0, Tn/n∈[ϵ,1−ϵ]T_{n}/n\in[\epsilon,1-\epsilon] almost surely and that ai≤ϵ​n/2a_{i}\leq\epsilon n/2. Then every fixed assignment pattern on AiA_{i} has probability exp⁡{−Θ⁡(ai)}\exp\{-\Theta(a_{i})\}, with constants depending only on ϵ\epsilon. Thus the same exp⁡{Θ⁡(di)}\exp\{\Theta(d_{i})\} inverse-propensity order holds for neighborhood DTE and TTE conditions, including the no-exposure and full-exposure count/fraction exposure representations. Fixed-size complete randomization is a special case when the treatment fraction is bounded away from zero and one.

In both cases, the inverse-propensity lower bound in Proposition 21 applies to any design-unbiased non-parametric estimator of the corresponding DTE or TTE. The exchangeable case covers local treatment–exposure combinations. It does not cover arbitrary-interference TTE/DTE targets under fixed nontrivial treatment fractions, because such designs put zero probability on the global all-treated or all-control assignments.

Proof of Proposition 41.

For the independent-design claim, fix a set AA with |A|=a|A|=a and a pattern zA∈{0,1}az_{A}\in\{0,1\}^{a}. If ϵ≤P⁡(Zk=1)≤1−ϵ\epsilon\leq P(Z_{k}=1)\leq 1-\epsilon for all kk, then

ϵa≤P⁡(𝐙A=zA)≤(1−ϵ)a.\epsilon^{a}\leq P(\mathbf{Z}_{A}=z_{A})\leq(1-\epsilon)^{a}.

For the bound, 𝔼⁡[Wi2]=2​(di+1)​{Yi​(1,𝟎Ni)2+Yi​(0,𝟎Ni)2}≤4​M2​(di+1)\mathbb{E}[W_{i}^{2}]=2(d_{i}+1)\{Y_{i}(1,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})^{2}+Y_{i}(0,\mathbf{0}_{N_{i}})^{2}\}\leq 4M^{2}(d_{i}+1), so Var⁡(Wi)≤4​M2​(di+1)\operatorname{Var}(W_{i})\leq 4M^{2}(d_{i}+1). E.4 Proof of Corollary 29

Proof.

On a dd-regular graph, ∑i(di+1)=n⁡(d+1)\sum_{i}(d_{i}+1)=n(d+1) and 2​|E|=n​d2|E|=nd. Each adjacent pair contributes at most 11, and each non-adjacent overlapping pair contributes si​j/(2​d+2−si​j)≤1s_{ij}/(2d+2-s_{ij})\leq 1 since si​j≤d−1s_{ij}\leq d-1, while each ordered wedge ∑kdk​(dk−1)=n​d​(d−1)\sum_{k}d_{k}(d_{k}-1)=nd(d-1) counts at most one non-adjacent overlapping pair. E.5 Proof of Lemma 30

Proof.

The event {i∈ℐ2}\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}\} is {Ui<Uk∀k∈Bi(2)∖{i}}\{U_{i}<U_{k}\ \forall k\in B_{i}^{(2)}\setminus\{i\}\}, i.e. UiU_{i} is the strict minimum among the bib_{i} independent draws in Bi(2)B_{i}^{(2)}; by exchangeability this has probability 1/bi1/b_{i}. On {i∈ℐ2,Ri=1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=1\}, step (3) sets the entire closed neighborhood to 11, giving (Zi,ZNi)=(1,𝟏)(Z_{i},Z_{N_{i}})=(1,\mathbf{1}), and RiR_{i} is independent of the draws, so ρi(1)=1/(2​bi)\rho_{i}^{(1)}=1/(2b_{i}); the control side is symmetric. The lower bound di+1≤bid_{i}+1\leq b_{i} holds because the closed neighborhood is contained in the radius-two ball. The upper bound follows by counting vertices reached from ii in zero, one, or two steps: at most 1+di+∑j∈Ni(dj−1)≤1+di​dmax1+d_{i}+\sum_{j\in N_{i}}(d_{j}-1)\leq 1+d_{i}d_{\max}. ∎

E.6 Proof of Proposition 31

Proof.

Unbiasedness follows directly from the focal reveal events. On {i∈ℐ2,Ri=1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=1\} the observed outcome equals Yi​(1,ei𝟏)Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}}), and on {i∈ℐ2,Ri=0}\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2},R_{i}=0\} it equals Yi​(0,0)Y_{i}(0,0); each event has probability 1/(2​bi)1/(2b_{i}). Writing τ^IST=n−1​∑iVi\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{IS}}^{T}=n^{-1}\sum_{i}V_{i}, the argument of Proposition 28 applies with pip_{i} replaced by qi=1/biq_{i}=1/b_{i} and δi\delta_{i} by Δi\Delta_{i}: conditioning on ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} gives 𝔼[Vi∣ℐ2]=𝟙{i∈ℐ2}Δi/qi\mathbb{E}[V_{i}\mid\mathcal{I}_{2}]=\mathds{1}\{i\in\mathcal{I}_{2}\}\Delta_{i}/q_{i} and, for i≠ji\neq j, Cov⁡(Vi,Vj)=Δi​Δj​(Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ2)/(qi​qj)−1)\operatorname{Cov}(V_{i},V_{j})=\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j}(\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I}_{2})/(q_{i}q_{j})-1). If Bi(2)∩Bj(2)=∅B_{i}^{(2)}\cap B_{j}^{(2)}=\emptyset the covariance vanishes. If distG​(i,j)≤2\mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\leq 2, then ii and jj cannot both be strict minima in their radius-two balls, so Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ2)=0\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I}_{2})=0. If distG​(i,j)∈{3,4}\mathrm{dist}_{G}(i,j)\in\{3,4\}, the same integral as before with ball sizes (bi,bj)(b_{i},b_{j}) and overlap s=si​j(2)s=s_{ij}^{(2)} gives Pr⁡(i,j∈ℐ2)/(qi​qj)=(bi+bj)/(bi+bj−s)\Pr(i,j\in\mathcal{I}_{2})/(q_{i}q_{j})=(b_{i}+b_{j})/(b_{i}+b_{j}-s). Finally 𝔼⁡[Vi2]=2​bi​{Yi​(1,ei𝟏)2+Yi​(0,0)2}≤4​M2​bi\mathbb{E}[V_{i}^{2}]=2b_{i}\{Y_{i}(1,e_{i}^{\mathbf{1}})^{2}+Y_{i}(0,0)^{2}\}\leq 4M^{2}b_{i}, and taking absolute values in the covariance sum gives the bound: distance-one and distance-two pairs contribute at most one each, and distance-three and distance-four overlapping pairs contribute si​j(2)/(bi+bj−si​j(2))s_{ij}^{(2)}/(b_{i}+b_{j}-s_{ij}^{(2)}). ∎

E.7 Proof of Corollary 32

Proof.

On a dd-regular locally tree-like graph, bi=1+d+d⁡(d−1)=d2+1b_{i}=1+d+d(d-1)=d^{2}+1, so the diagonal term is 4​M2​n−2​∑ibi=O⁡(M2​d2/n)4M^{2}n^{-2}\sum_{i}b_{i}=O(M^{2}d^{2}/n). The number of ordered pairs at distance at most two is O⁡(n​d2)O(nd^{2}), so the distance-two exclusion term is also O⁡(M2​d2/n)O(M^{2}d^{2}/n). For the positive radius-two overlap term, each unit has at most d​(d−1)2d(d-1)^{2} distance-three partners, each with overlap s=2s=2 and denominator of order d2d^{2}, contributing O⁡(n​d)O(nd); each unit has O⁡(d4)O(d^{4}) distance-four partners, each with overlap s=1s=1 and denominator of order d2d^{2}, contributing O⁡(n​d2)O(nd^{2}), which is the same order as the diagonal and exclusion terms. Thus the total is O⁡(M2​d2/n)O(M^{2}d^{2}/n). For a general graph, the diagonal and distance-two exclusion terms are bounded by O⁡(∑ibi)O(\sum_{i}b_{i}), and wedge-counting in the radius-two overlap graph bounds the positive overlap sum by ∑kbk​(bk−1)\sum_{k}b_{k}(b_{k}-1), giving O⁡(M2​b2¯/n)O(M^{2}\overline{b^{2}}/n). ∎

Proof.

Taking s=1−qs=1-q gives 𝔼⁡[(1−q)Ki]→e−q\mathbb{E}[(1-q)^{K_{i}}]\to e^{-q}; hence ρi(1)→1−e−q\rho_{i}^{(1)}\to 1-e^{-q}, and since q/(d+1)→0q/(d+1)\to 0, ρi(0)→e−q\rho_{i}^{(0)}\to e^{-q}.

Star center. For the center cc of a star, the leaves are degree-one units: given Uc=uU_{c}=u, each leaf is an ego exactly when its single draw falls below uu, so the leaf ego events are independent Bernoulli(uu) and

𝔼⁡[(1−q)Kc]=∫01(1−q​u)d​𝑑u=1−(1−q)d+1q⁡(d+1)=O⁡(1q​d),\mathbb{E}[(1-q)^{K_{c}}]=\int_{0}^{1}(1-qu)^{d}\,du=\frac{1-(1-q)^{d+1}}{q(d+1)}=O\!\Big(\frac{1}{qd}\Big),
